question.stem:
A 68-year-old man with COPD (FEV1 38% predicted) is brought to the ED for 3 days of worsening dyspnea and increased purulent sputum. He ran out of his home oxygen 2 weeks ago. He has already received nebulized albuterol-ipratropium, IV methylprednisolone, and levofloxacin, but remains tachypneic and fatigued.

Temperature 37.1 C, BP 145/90 mm Hg, HR 112/min, RR 32/min, SpO2 90% on 4 L nasal cannula. He is alert, speaking in 3-4 word sentences, using accessory muscles, with diffuse expiratory wheezing.

Arterial blood gas on 4 L nasal cannula: pH 7.29, PaCO2 68 mm Hg, PaO2 58 mm Hg, HCO3 26 mEq/L. He remains cooperative and hemodynamically stable.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Increase supplemental oxygen to target SpO2 96-100%
Intubate and start invasive mechanical ventilation
Observe with serial ABGs and reassess in 2 hours

question.explanation: Per GOLD 2025, noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) is the first-line intervention for AECOPD with acute or acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35, PaCO2 >45 mm Hg) in a patient who is alert and hemodynamically stable, reducing need for intubation and improving mortality [1,2]. This patient has persistent respiratory acidosis despite maximal medical therapy but retains adequate mental status and hemodynamics, making him an ideal NIV candidate rather than requiring immediate intubation. Reserve invasive ventilation for NIV failure or contraindications (decreased consciousness not attributable to hypercapnia, hemodynamic instability, inability to protect the airway, facial trauma, copious secretions). Note also that oxygen should be titrated to SpO2 88-92%, not normalized to 96-100%, because over-oxygenation worsens hypercapnia via V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect, and reduction of hypoxic ventilatory drive [1,3].

wrong_explanations.why: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index, frequent toxicity, and no proven mortality or intubation-avoidance benefit in AECOPD; it is not recommended by GOLD as acute therapy.
Raising SpO2 to 96-100% in COPD worsens hypercapnia via V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect; target SpO2 is 88-92%, not near-normal saturation.
Immediate intubation is reserved for NIV failure or contraindications (altered consciousness, hemodynamic instability, inability to protect airway); this alert, stable patient should first trial NIV.
Delaying therapy risks progressive acidosis and respiratory arrest; worsening pH with persistent tachypnea mandates immediate ventilatory support, not watchful waiting.

question.difficulty_rationale: Requires integrating ABG data, mental status/hemodynamic stability, and current oxygenation target to select NIV over both under-treatment (observation, theophylline, excess oxygen) and over-treatment (immediate intubation).
reasoning_steps: Recognize acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure with respiratory acidosis (pH 7.29, PaCO2 68) despite maximal bronchodilator/steroid/antibiotic therapy
Assess mental status and hemodynamics to determine NIV candidacy - patient is alert, cooperative, and stable, favoring NIV over intubation
Apply GOLD 2025 recommendation that NIV is first-line for AECOPD with pH <7.35 and PaCO2 >45 mm Hg, reducing intubation and mortality
Recognize the oxygen-target trap - increasing FiO2 to normalize SpO2 would worsen hypercapnia via V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect
Eliminate theophylline (no acute benefit, toxicity risk) and observation (delays needed ventilatory support in worsening acidosis)

talk.key_point: In AECOPD with respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35), noninvasive ventilation is first-line in alert, hemodynamically stable patients, and supplemental oxygen should target SpO2 88-92%, not normalization.
board_pearls: NIV reduces work of breathing and offloads fatigued respiratory muscles, correcting alveolar hypoventilation without the risks of intubation.
GOLD 2025 recommends NIV as first-line for AECOPD with acute or acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35, PaCO2 >45 mm Hg) [1].
The key discriminator between NIV and intubation is mental status and hemodynamic stability - an alert, cooperative patient favors NIV; obtundation or shock mandates intubation.
Landmark trials (Brochard 1995 NEJM) established that NIV reduces intubation rates and mortality in AECOPD respiratory failure [2].
The most common trap is escalating oxygen to normalize SpO2; COPD patients should be titrated to SpO2 88-92% to avoid worsening hypercapnia via V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect [1,3].
teaching_points: NIV is guideline-preferred first-line ventilatory support in AECOPD with acute respiratory acidosis, superior to early intubation in appropriate candidates.
Oxygen titration targets in COPD (88-92%) differ from general critical illness targets, reflecting the risk of worsening hypercapnia with hyperoxia.
Contraindications to NIV (impaired consciousness from causes other than hypercapnia, hemodynamic instability, inability to protect airway, copious secretions) should prompt direct intubation instead.
summary_points: In stable, alert AECOPD patients with respiratory acidosis unresponsive to initial medical therapy, initiate NIV before considering intubation, and keep SpO2 targets at 88-92%.

talk.subtitle: Choosing ventilatory support after maximal medical therapy — GOLD 2025

question.stem:
A 68-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department for 3 days of worsening dyspnea with increased sputum volume and purulence. He has GOLD group E COPD (FEV1 42% predicted) with two exacerbations in the past year and continues to smoke. Over the past hour he has received nebulized albuterol-ipratropium every 20 minutes, IV methylprednisolone 40 mg, and oral azithromycin. Oxygen was titrated to 2 L/min by nasal cannula.

Temperature 37.4 C, BP 138/84 mm Hg, HR 104/min, RR 28/min, SpO2 90% on 2 L/min. He is alert, oriented, and speaking in short phrases, using accessory muscles, with diffuse expiratory wheeze and prolonged expiration. There is no jugular venous distention or peripheral edema.

ABG on 2 L/min: pH 7.27, PaCO2 64 mm Hg, PaO2 62 mm Hg, bicarbonate 28 mEq/L. CXR shows hyperinflation without infiltrate or pneumothorax. BNP 60 pg/mL.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Increase FiO2 to target SpO2 above 94%
Perform endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
Start intravenous methylprednisolone 125 mg every 6 hours

question.explanation:
GOLD 2025 states that noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is the first-line mode of ventilatory support in acute exacerbations of COPD complicated by acute or acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure, with indications of respiratory acidosis (pH <=7.35 with PaCO2 >45 mm Hg), severe dyspnea with signs of increased work of breathing, or persistent hypoxemia despite supplemental oxygen. NIV improves gas exchange and reduces work of breathing, intubation rate, length of stay, and mortality [1,2,3].

This patient satisfies those criteria: pH 7.27 with PaCO2 64 mm Hg and only modest bicarbonate elevation indicates acute-on-chronic hypercapnia, and he has tachypnea with accessory muscle use despite one hour of maximal bronchodilator, systemic corticosteroid, and antibiotic therapy (his Anthonisen cardinal symptoms — increased dyspnea, sputum volume, and sputum purulence — justify the antibiotic) [4]. Crucially, he has no contraindication to NIV: he is alert, cooperative, hemodynamically stable, able to protect his airway, and has no pneumothorax, facial trauma, or vomiting. Oxygenation is already appropriate for COPD (target SpO2 88-92%), so the problem to be fixed is ventilation, not oxygen delivery.

Alternative diagnoses that would change management are excluded by the vignette: BNP 60 pg/mL and absent edema/JVD argue against decompensated heart failure, and the CXR excludes pneumonia and pneumothorax. Therefore, adding NIV — with close monitoring for failure (worsening pH/PaCO2, deteriorating mental status, hemodynamic instability), at which point intubation is indicated — is the correct next step.

wrong_explanations.why: IV magnesium is an adjunct in severe acute asthma with poor bronchodilator response; there is no GOLD recommendation for magnesium in COPD exacerbation, and it does not address hypercapnic respiratory failure.

Targeting SpO2 >94% risks worsening hypercapnia through loss of hypoxic vasoconstriction, Haldane effect, and reduced drive. GOLD advises titration to SpO2 88-92%; his SpO2 of 90% is already at target.

Intubation is reserved for NIV failure or contraindications (impaired consciousness, inability to protect the airway, hemodynamic instability, arrest). He is alert and cooperative, so a trial of NIV should precede invasive ventilation.

High-dose IV steroids offer no benefit over 40 mg prednisone-equivalent daily for 5 days and add hyperglycemia and myopathy risk. Escalating steroid dose will not correct acute respiratory acidosis in the next hour.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must recognize acute-on-chronic hypercapnic acidosis after maximal medical therapy, verify the absence of ventilatory-support contraindications, and then choose between two closely competing modes of respiratory support while rejecting oxygen and pharmacologic escalation.
reasoning_steps: Identify an AECOPD with all three Anthonisen cardinal symptoms; note bronchodilators, systemic steroid, and antibiotic have already been given.
Interpret the ABG: pH 7.27 with PaCO2 64 and bicarbonate only 28 mEq/L = acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis, not compensated chronic hypercapnia.
Exclude competing causes of decompensation: normal BNP with no edema/JVD argues against HF; CXR excludes pneumonia and pneumothorax.
Apply GOLD 2025: pH <=7.35 with PaCO2 >45 plus increased work of breathing is a first-line indication for NIV.
Confirm no contraindication to NIV (alert, cooperative, hemodynamically stable, airway protected), so invasive ventilation is not yet required.

talk.key_point: In a COPD exacerbation with pH <=7.35 and PaCO2 >45 mm Hg, start NIV first-line if the patient is alert and protecting the airway; reserve intubation for NIV failure or contraindication. [1]
board_pearls: NIV (inspiratory pressure support plus PEEP) unloads the inspiratory muscles and counteracts intrinsic PEEP from dynamic hyperinflation, increasing alveolar ventilation and correcting respiratory acidosis without an artificial airway.

GOLD 2025 lists respiratory acidosis (pH <=7.35 with PaCO2 >45 mm Hg), severe dyspnea with increased work of breathing, and persistent hypoxemia as indications for NIV in AECOPD; NIV is explicitly the first mode of ventilation. [1]

The discriminator between NIV and intubation is mental status and airway protection: an alert, cooperative, hemodynamically stable patient gets a monitored NIV trial; obtundation, aspiration risk, or shock mandates intubation. [1]
Brochard (NEJM 1995) and Plant (Lancet 2000) showed NIV in AECOPD reduces intubation rate, complications, hospital stay, and mortality — the evidence base behind the GOLD recommendation. [2,3]
The commonest trap is chasing the SpO2: raising FiO2 to >94% in hypercapnic COPD worsens CO2 retention; target SpO2 88-92% and treat the ventilation problem, not the oximeter.

abim_classification.specific_topic: COPD exacerbation: NIV for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure

teaching_points: Anthonisen cardinal symptoms (increased dyspnea, sputum volume, sputum purulence) guide antibiotics in AECOPD; antibiotics are also indicated for patients requiring mechanical ventilation, invasive or noninvasive. [1,4]
Systemic corticosteroids for AECOPD: prednisone 40 mg daily (or equivalent) for 5 days — higher doses and longer courses add toxicity without added benefit. [1]

Reassess ABG and clinical trajectory 1-2 hours after starting NIV; failure to improve pH/PaCO2, worsening encephalopathy, or hemodynamic instability should prompt intubation rather than prolonged NIV.
summary_points: Acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure in AECOPD, in an alert patient who has already received bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics, is treated with NIV as first-line ventilatory support. [1]

visual_memory_card.bottom_left: pH <=7.35 + PaCO2 >45 in AECOPD: NIV

gemini_errors: ABG is internally inconsistent: pH 7.29 with PaCO2 68 mm Hg and HCO3 26 mEq/L is not physiologically possible (Henderson-Hasselbalch yields pH ≈7.21; a pH of 7.29 at PaCO2 68 requires HCO3 ≈31-32). Boards-style vignettes must have coherent gas values, and the stated HCO3 also undercuts the 'acute-on-chronic' framing.

Cites the Nocturnal Oxygen Therapy Trial (NOTT 1980) in support of an acute SpO2 target of 88-92% and hyperoxia-induced hypercapnia (Haldane effect/V-Q mismatch). NOTT addressed long-term home oxygen for chronic severe hypoxemia and mortality; it does not support acute titration targets or the hyperoxic hypercapnia mechanism — a citation the source would not support.
States the GOLD NIV threshold as 'pH <7.35'; GOLD 2025 specifies pH ≤7.35 with PaCO2 >45 mm Hg (minor overstatement/imprecision).
claude_errors: Memory-card phrasing 'Raising FiO2 above 92% worsens hypercapnia' conflates FiO2 with SpO2 (imprecise rather than substantively wrong).
judge.why: Both correctly identify NIV as first-line for AECOPD with acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure in an alert, hemodynamically stable patient, and both correctly flag the hyperoxia trap and the SpO2 88-92% target. B is superior on all four graded dimensions: its ABG is internally consistent and truly reflects acute-on-chronic acidosis (pH 7.27/PaCO2 64/HCO3 28), it quotes the GOLD 2025 NIV indications with the correct threshold (pH ≤7.35 + PaCO2 >45) without inflating recommendation strength, and every citation is used for a claim the source actually supports (Brochard and Plant for intubation/mortality benefit, Anthonisen for cardinal symptoms guiding antibiotics). B also adds higher teaching yield — mimic exclusion (BNP, CXR), the 40 mg x 5 days steroid standard, antibiotics for patients requiring ventilatory support, and the mandate to recheck ABG at 1-2 hours with intubation for NIV failure. A's key weaknesses are a physiologically impossible ABG and attributing acute oxygen-titration/Haldane teaching to NOTT, a trial about long-term oxygen therapy — a citation-honesty error that matters when residents are taught to trace claims to sources. A's distractors (theophylline, observation) are also somewhat softer than B's more discriminating options (magnesium, high-dose steroids).

Every risk marker is downstream of RV mechanics, not the clot itself.","teaching_pearl":"Think of PE mortality as a right heart failure problem, not a lung problem — clot burden matters far less than whether the RV can tolerate the afterload it's just been handed.","board_tip":"McConnell sign (akinetic RV free wall with a spared, hyperkinetic apex) is a classic echo pearl for acute RV strain from PE — distinguishes it from chronic RV pressure overload where the whole RV is hypertrophied and uniformly dysfunctional."},{"heading":"Risk Stratification Frameworks: Old vs New Taxonomy","minutes":"3 min","points":["The 2026 AHA/ACC Acute PE Guideline is the first dedicated US PE guideline and RETIRES the 'massive/submassive/non-massive' vocabulary, replacing it with Acute PE Clinical Categories A through E with subcategories based on hemodynamics, RV function, and biomarkers [1].","ESC 2019 has not been reissued and remains the current European reference, using the parallel four-tier strata: low-risk, intermediate-low-risk, intermediate-high-risk, and high-risk [2] — know both systems and be explicit about which one you're using on rounds.","Clinical risk score: simplified PESI (sPESI) — age >80, cancer, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, HR ≥110, SBP <100, SpO2 <90%; a score of 0 identifies low-risk patients who can be considered for outpatient management.","Hemodynamic assessment is the first branch point in both systems: sustained hypotension (SBP <90 for 15+ min) or cardiac arrest = the highest-risk tier regardless of biomarkers or imaging (old 'massive'; now AHA/ACC's highest lettered category).","RV dysfunction (by echo or CT RV/LV ratio >0.9) PLUS an elevated biomarker (troponin or BNP) defines the intermediate-high risk tier — this is the group at real risk for hemodynamic decompensation in the next 24-72h even while normotensive."],"mechanism":"Biomarkers and imaging are surrogate readouts of the same RV-afterload cascade described above — troponin/BNP quantify the physiologic insult, while echo/CT quantify the anatomic consequence. Combining a clinical score (sPESI) with an anatomic/biomarker read (RV function + troponin) captures both the patient's physiologic reserve and the acute RV injury, which is why current risk models require both.","teaching_pearl":"Normotensive does not mean low-risk — a normotensive patient with RV dilation and a positive troponin is physiologically closer to the high-risk group than to a true low-risk PE, because they're one septal-shift event away from decompensating.","board_tip":"On boards, if you see 'PE + hypotension' = high-risk/Category E regardless of anything else. If you see 'PE + normotensive + RV dysfunction + positive troponin' = intermediate-high risk — the classic trick answer is to call this patient 'stable' and undertreat them."},{"heading":"Workup: What Each Test Is Actually Answering","minutes":"2 min","points":["CTA chest with contrast is the diagnostic test of choice for confirming clot burden and directly visualizing RV/LV ratio as an anatomic marker of strain.","Troponin and BNP/NT-proBNP are drawn in every confirmed PE to detect subclinical RV injury/strain even when hemodynamics look reassuring — they answer 'is the RV already hurting?'","Bedside echo (or formal echo if time allows) answers the same RV question with functional detail — TAPSE, McConnell sign, septal flattening — and is preferred when the patient is too unstable for CT.","The YEARS algorithm adapts the D-dimer cutoff to pretest probability, reducing unnecessary CTA imaging in low pretest probability patients while still safely excluding PE [1].","sPESI is calculated on every confirmed PE regardless of imaging findings — it is the clinical layer that, combined with imaging/biomarkers, determines disposition (outpatient DOAC vs monitored admission vs ICU)."],"teaching_pearl":"Order troponin/BNP and echo on every hemodynamically stable PE, not just the ones that 'look sick' — subclinical RV strain is common and changes your monitoring plan even when the patient is talking to you normally."},{"heading":"Treatment by Risk Tier — Mechanism-Matched Therapy","minutes":"3 min","points":["High-risk / Category E (shock or arrest): systemic thrombolysis, alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours — mechanism is plasminogen activation to rapidly lyse clot and drop PVR before RV ischemia becomes irreversible; bleeding risk must be weighed per PEITHO-informed data [4]. sections.heading: Physiology & Pathophysiology: Why the RV Is the Whole Story
points: A thrombus lodges in the pulmonary arterial tree → acute mechanical obstruction of pulmonary vascular bed, amplified by hypoxic vasoconstriction and platelet-released serotonin/thromboxane A2 → sudden rise in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR).
The RV is a thin-walled, low-pressure chamber built for volume, not pressure, work — it cannot acutely compensate for a PVR spike the way the LV tolerates afterload.

Acute RV afterload → RV dilation → increased RV wall tension (Laplace's law) → increased RV oxygen demand at the same time coronary perfusion pressure falls, because RV subendocardial perfusion depends on a favorable aortic-to-RV pressure gradient that collapses as RV pressure rises toward systemic levels.

The dilated RV bows the interventricular septum leftward (interventricular dependence), reducing LV preload and compliance → falls in LV stroke volume and cardiac output → systemic hypotension, and in the worst cases, obstructive shock and cardiac arrest.

This single cascade — PVR rise → RV strain/ischemia → septal shift → LV underfilling — is the mechanistic thread that every clinical finding, biomarker, and imaging sign in PE risk stratification is built on.
sections.mechanism: Elevated troponin reflects RV microinfarction/strain from the supply-demand mismatch above; elevated BNP/NT-proBNP reflects RV wall stress from acute dilation; echo/CT RV dilation and septal flattening are the direct anatomic read-out of interventricular dependence. Every risk marker is downstream of RV mechanics, not the clot itself.
sections.teaching_pearl: Think of PE mortality as a right heart failure problem, not a lung problem — clot burden matters far less than whether the RV can tolerate the afterload it's just been handed.
sections.board_tip: McConnell sign (akinetic RV free wall with a spared, hyperkinetic apex) is a classic echo pearl for acute RV strain from PE — distinguishes it from chronic RV pressure overload where the whole RV is hypertrophied and uniformly dysfunctional.

sections.heading: Risk Stratification Frameworks: Old vs New Taxonomy
points: The 2026 AHA/ACC Acute PE Guideline is the first dedicated US PE guideline and RETIRES the 'massive/submassive/non-massive' vocabulary, replacing it with Acute PE Clinical Categories A through E with subcategories based on hemodynamics, RV function, and biomarkers [1].

ESC 2019 has not been reissued and remains the current European reference, using the parallel four-tier strata: low-risk, intermediate-low-risk, intermediate-high-risk, and high-risk [2] — know both systems and be explicit about which one you're using on rounds.

Clinical risk score: simplified PESI (sPESI) — age >80, cancer, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, HR ≥110, SBP <100, SpO2 <90%; a score of 0 identifies low-risk patients who can be considered for outpatient management.

Hemodynamic assessment is the first branch point in both systems: sustained hypotension (SBP <90 for 15+ min) or cardiac arrest = the highest-risk tier regardless of biomarkers or imaging (old 'massive'; now AHA/ACC's highest lettered category).

RV dysfunction (by echo or CT RV/LV ratio >0.9) PLUS an elevated biomarker (troponin or BNP) defines the intermediate-high risk tier — this is the group at real risk for hemodynamic decompensation in the next 24-72h even while normotensive.
sections.mechanism: Biomarkers and imaging are surrogate readouts of the same RV-afterload cascade described above — troponin/BNP quantify the physiologic insult, while echo/CT quantify the anatomic consequence. Combining a clinical score (sPESI) with an anatomic/biomarker read (RV function + troponin) captures both the patient's physiologic reserve and the acute RV injury, which is why current risk models require both.
sections.teaching_pearl: Normotensive does not mean low-risk — a normotensive patient with RV dilation and a positive troponin is physiologically closer to the high-risk group than to a true low-risk PE, because they're one septal-shift event away from decompensating.
sections.board_tip: On boards, if you see 'PE + hypotension' = high-risk/Category E regardless of anything else. If you see 'PE + normotensive + RV dysfunction + positive troponin' = intermediate-high risk — the classic trick answer is to call this patient 'stable' and undertreat them.

sections.heading: Workup: What Each Test Is Actually Answering
points: CTA chest with contrast is the diagnostic test of choice for confirming clot burden and directly visualizing RV/LV ratio as an anatomic marker of strain.
Troponin and BNP/NT-proBNP are drawn in every confirmed PE to detect subclinical RV injury/strain even when hemodynamics look reassuring — they answer 'is the RV already hurting?'
Bedside echo (or formal echo if time allows) answers the same RV question with functional detail — TAPSE, McConnell sign, septal flattening — and is preferred when the patient is too unstable for CT.
The YEARS algorithm adapts the D-dimer cutoff to pretest probability, reducing unnecessary CTA imaging in low pretest probability patients while still safely excluding PE [1].

sPESI is calculated on every confirmed PE regardless of imaging findings — it is the clinical layer that, combined with imaging/biomarkers, determines disposition (outpatient DOAC vs monitored admission vs ICU).
sections.teaching_pearl: Order troponin/BNP and echo on every hemodynamically stable PE, not just the ones that 'look sick' — subclinical RV strain is common and changes your monitoring plan even when the patient is talking to you normally.

sections.heading: Treatment by Risk Tier — Mechanism-Matched Therapy
points: High-risk / Category E (shock or arrest): systemic thrombolysis, alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours — mechanism is plasminogen activation to rapidly lyse clot and drop PVR before RV ischemia becomes irreversible; bleeding risk must be weighed per PEITHO-informed data [4]. Catheter-directed or surgical embolectomy if lysis is contraindicated [1].

Intermediate-high risk (RV dysfunction + positive biomarker, normotensive): admit for 48-72h of close monitoring with rescue thrombolysis available if decompensation occurs — PEITHO showed systemic lysis in this group reduced hemodynamic decompensation but increased major bleeding/ICH with no mortality benefit, so lysis is reserved for rescue, not routine, in this tier [4].

Catheter-directed thrombolysis for intermediate-high risk is TRIAL EVIDENCE ONLY at this stage — ULTIMA showed improved RV/LV ratio at 24h [8], and PE-TRACT is an ongoing/evolving randomized trial testing catheter-based thrombus removal against anticoagulation alone; neither the 2026 AHA/ACC nor ESC 2019 has yet made this a preferred first-line intervention over anticoagulation [1,9].
Low-risk (sPESI 0): outpatient management on a DOAC is guideline-supported — HoT-PE prospectively validated this strategy with a low VTE recurrence/death rate in carefully selected patients [5].

Anticoagulant choice per CHEST/ACCP 2021: apixaban and rivaroxaban are preferred as single-drug (no parenteral lead-in) regimens; dabigatran and edoxaban require a parenteral lead-in [3]. Exceptions favoring LMWH/warfarin: CrCl <30, triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome, mechanical heart valves [3]. Duration is at least 3 months for a provoked PE; indefinite low-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BID or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for unprovoked/persistent risk factor, per AMPLIFY-EXT/EINSTEIN-CHOICE [3,6,7].
sections.mechanism: Thrombolytics work by converting plasminogen to plasmin, dissolving the obstructing clot and acutely lowering PVR — this directly reverses the RV-afterload cascade from section 1, which is why it's reserved for tiers where RV ischemia/failure is imminent or established, and why the bleeding-risk tradeoff only favors lysis once the RV is genuinely failing rather than merely strained.
sections.teaching_pearl: The intermediate-high risk patient is the hardest board question and the hardest real patient — they look stable in front of you but PEITHO taught us that early aggressive lysis trades decompensation risk for bleeding risk with no net mortality gain, so 'watch closely, treat if they crash' is the correct answer, not 'lyse everyone with a positive troponin.'
sections.board_tip: If asked to compare terminologies: 'massive/submassive' = old ESC-adjacent language now RETIRED by 2026 AHA/ACC in favor of Categories A-E; ESC 2019 still uses low/intermediate-low/intermediate-high/high — state explicitly which system you are using so you aren't marked wrong for mixing vocabularies [1,2].

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: High-risk PE with shock or cardiac arrest carries a reported mortality in the range of 25-65%, driven almost entirely by RV failure and cardiogenic shock physiology described above.

Intermediate-high risk PE (RV dysfunction + positive biomarker, normotensive) carries roughly a 3-15% risk of adverse outcome including hemodynamic decompensation or death, which is why 48-72h of monitoring is mandated even in a 'stable-appearing' patient.
Low-risk PE (sPESI 0) carries under 1% 30-day mortality, supporting outpatient DOAC management validated in HoT-PE [5].

The single strongest driver of prognosis is RV function, not clot burden on CT — a large clot with a compensated RV can do well, while a small clot in a patient with limited cardiopulmonary reserve can decompensate.
sections.teaching_pearl: When a resident asks 'how big is the clot' as their first risk-stratification question, redirect them: the RV's response to the clot, not the clot's size, is what predicts the patient's course.

summary_points: PE mortality physiology is an RV-afterload story: PVR rises acutely, the thin-walled RV dilates and ischemic, the septum shifts left, and LV output falls — every risk marker (troponin, BNP, RV/LV ratio, McConnell sign) is a readout of this single cascade.

The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline retires 'massive/submassive' language for Clinical Categories A-E, while ESC 2019 (not yet reissued) still uses low/intermediate-low/intermediate-high/high — name which taxonomy you're using [1,2].

High-risk (shock/arrest) gets systemic thrombolysis or embolectomy; intermediate-high risk gets monitoring with rescue lysis reserved for decompensation (PEITHO) [4]; low-risk (sPESI 0) can go home on a DOAC (HoT-PE) [5].

Apixaban and rivaroxaban are preferred single-drug DOAC regimens per CHEST/ACCP 2021; treat at least 3 months, indefinitely if unprovoked, using low-dose extended regimens validated by AMPLIFY-EXT and EINSTEIN-CHOICE [3,6,7].

The most common pitfall: labeling a normotensive patient with RV dysfunction and a positive troponin as 'low-risk' because their blood pressure looks fine — this intermediate-high group needs monitored admission, not discharge.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis is promising (ULTIMA) but remains trial evidence only pending PE-TRACT results — it is not yet a guideline-preferred first-line strategy over anticoagulation for intermediate-risk PE [8,9].

sections.heading: Physiology: PE kills through the right ventricle, not the lung
points: Clot obstructs the pulmonary arterial bed, but mechanical obstruction is only part of the afterload rise: platelet-derived thromboxane A2 and serotonin plus local hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction cause reflex vasoconstriction in non-occluded segments, so pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) rises out of proportion to angiographic clot burden.

The normal RV is a thin-walled volume pump built for a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) of ~15 mmHg. An unconditioned RV cannot acutely generate an mPAP much above 40 mmHg — so an mPAP of 50 in an acute PE tells you the RV is not acute (chronic disease/CTEPH), and a 'normal' pressure can still be lethal if the RV has already failed.

Afterload mismatch → RV dilation → rising RV wall tension (Laplace) → rising RV oxygen demand at the exact moment supply falls. The RV free wall is normally perfused by the RCA in both systole and diastole; when systemic pressure drops and RV cavity/wall pressure rises, that transmural gradient collapses and the RV becomes ischemic. This is why troponin is positive in PE without coronary disease.

Interventricular dependence closes the loop: the dilated RV shifts the septum leftward inside a non-compliant pericardium, reducing LV diastolic filling. LV preload falls → cardiac output falls → coronary perfusion pressure falls → more RV ischemia. That is the PE death spiral, and it is why fluid loading a dilated RV makes patients worse.

Gas exchange derangements are the noisy epiphenomena: increased dead space, V/Q mismatch, right-to-left shunt through atelectatic/low-V/Q units and occasionally a patent foramen ovale. Early on, tachypnea produces hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis; a rising PaCO2 in acute PE is a late, ominous sign of exhaustion or profound low output.

BNP/NT-proBNP reflects myocyte stretch (RV wall stress); troponin reflects RV micronecrosis. Together with imaging of RV size/function they are the biological readout of the physiology above — which is precisely why all modern risk models are built from hemodynamics + RV imaging + biomarkers.
sections.mechanism: Every element of PE risk stratification is a surrogate for one variable: how much afterload the RV is absorbing and whether it is still compensating. Hemodynamics measure output, echo/CT measure RV geometry, troponin measures RV ischemia, BNP measures RV wall stress.
sections.teaching_pearl: Hypoxemia does not stratify PE risk — RV function does. A hypoxemic patient with a normal RV is low risk; a normoxemic patient with a dilated, hypokinetic RV and positive troponin is not.
sections.board_tip: Syncope in PE is a hemodynamic sign (transient RV output failure), not a neurologic one — it should push you toward, not away from, a higher-risk category.

sections.heading: The taxonomy: 2026 AHA/ACC categories A–E vs ESC 2019 strata — say which you are using
points: The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline is the first dedicated US PE guideline and its headline change is nomenclature: acute PE clinical categories A through E with subcategories, arranged by increasing severity, and the words 'massive' and 'submassive' are RETIRED. Use the categories in US documentation and know that submassive is now obsolete vocabulary. [1]

ESC 2019 has NOT been reissued and remains the European standard with four strata: low, intermediate-low, intermediate-high, and high risk. Name your taxonomy explicitly when you present a patient — the two systems are parallel, not identical. [1,2]

The operational inputs are unchanged across both systems: (1) hemodynamics — sustained hypotension, shock, arrest; (2) clinical score — PESI class or sPESI; (3) RV dysfunction — echo (RV/LV ratio, TAPSE, McConnell sign) or CT (RV/LV diameter ratio ≥0.9–1.0); (4) cardiac troponin. [1,2]

sPESI (each 1 point): age >80, cancer, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, HR ≥110, systolic BP <100, SpO2 <90%. Score 0 = low risk with a 30-day mortality around 1% and is the gate to outpatient management. [4]

ESC operational definitions worth memorizing: HIGH risk = hemodynamic instability (arrest, obstructive shock, or persistent hypotension) regardless of scores. INTERMEDIATE-HIGH = hemodynamically stable but BOTH RV dysfunction on imaging AND elevated troponin. INTERMEDIATE-LOW = one or neither positive with elevated PESI/sPESI. LOW = sPESI 0 with no RV dysfunction. [2]

Diagnosis feeds stratification: the YEARS algorithm adapts the D-dimer threshold to pretest probability (500 ng/mL with any YEARS item, 1000 ng/mL with none), safely reducing CT use. Once you have the CT, read the RV/LV ratio — it is free risk stratification. [1,8]
sections.mechanism: The four inputs are sequenced from most to least downstream: hypotension means the RV has already failed, RV dilation means it is failing, troponin means it is ischemic but compensating, and sPESI captures the reserve the patient brought to the event.
sections.teaching_pearl: A 'normal-sized' clot with a dilated RV is a sicker patient than a large-looking clot with a normal RV. Stop grading PE by clot bulk on the CT report.
sections.board_tip: Hemodynamic instability trumps everything. If the patient is in shock or arrest, do not calculate sPESI — they are high-risk/most severe category by definition. [2]

sections.heading: Management follows the category — and the risk of the drug follows the risk of the clot
points: HIGH RISK (shock/arrest): systemic thrombolysis — alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours — is guideline-recommended; catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy when lysis is contraindicated or fails. Do not withhold lysis in true shock while waiting for confirmatory testing if the diagnosis is highly probable. [1]

INTERMEDIATE-HIGH (stable but RV dysfunction + positive troponin): therapeutic anticoagulation with monitoring for 48–72 hours in a setting capable of RESCUE thrombolysis on decompensation. This is the single highest-yield management point in PE. [1,2]

Why not lyse them up front? PEITHO randomized 1,006 intermediate-risk patients (RV dysfunction + positive troponin) to tenecteplase vs placebo: hemodynamic decompensation fell (5.6% → 2.6%) but major extracranial bleeding rose (~6.3% vs 1.2%) and intracranial hemorrhage occurred in ~2% with no mortality benefit. Net harm at the population level — hence 'monitor with rescue lysis.' [3]

Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) and mechanical thrombectomy are EVOLVING, not settled: ULTIMA showed ultrasound-assisted CDT improved RV/LV ratio at 24 h vs heparin alone but was not powered for clinical outcomes, and the definitive trial (PE-TRACT) is ongoing. Present CDT as reasonable in selected intermediate-high patients at experienced centers/PERT, not as standard of care. [1,6,9]

LOW RISK (sPESI 0, no RV dysfunction, adequate social support and follow-up): outpatient treatment with a DOAC. HoT-PE treated low-risk PE at home with rivaroxaban and found recurrent VTE ~0.6% at 3 months. Apixaban and rivaroxaban are single-drug regimens; dabigatran and edoxaban require a parenteral lead-in of ≥5 days. [1,5,7]

Anticoagulation duration: at least 3 months for all. Provoked by a transient major risk factor → stop at 3 months. Unprovoked or persistent risk factor → extended therapy, with reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BID or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily as options (AMPLIFY-EXT, EINSTEIN-CHOICE). Favor LMWH/warfarin over DOACs in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome, CrCl <30, and mechanical valves. Cancer-associated VTE: apixaban or edoxaban preferred, avoiding edoxaban/rivaroxaban with luminal GI tumors. [7]
sections.mechanism: Thrombolytics activate plasminogen to plasmin, cleaving cross-linked fibrin and rapidly unloading the RV — but plasmin is indiscriminate and lyses hemostatic plugs everywhere, so the benefit scales with how close the RV is to failing while the bleeding hazard is roughly fixed. That asymmetry is exactly why lysis wins in shock and loses in stable intermediate-risk PE. Anticoagulants do not dissolve clot; they prevent propagation and let endogenous fibrinolysis work.
sections.teaching_pearl: 'Rescue lysis' means having a plan written in the note: what vital sign triggers it, who to call, and where the alteplase is. An intermediate-high PE on a telemetry floor without that plan is under-managed.
sections.board_tip: Vasopressors, not fluids, for the hypotensive PE patient — norepinephrine supports coronary perfusion pressure to the ischemic RV. Aggressive volume loading distends the RV, worsens septal shift, and drops LV output.

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: Mortality tracks the category almost linearly: high-risk PE with shock or arrest carries short-term mortality in the range of 25–50% or higher; intermediate-high roughly 5–15%; intermediate-low a few percent; low risk (sPESI 0) ~1% at 30 days. [2,4]

Decompensation risk defines the intermediate-high group: in PEITHO, placebo-arm hemodynamic collapse was 5.6% within 7 days — small enough that routine lysis is net harmful, large enough that these patients require monitored beds. [3]

Prognosis is driven by RV function and comorbidity, not clot size. Persistent RV dysfunction, elevated troponin/lactate, syncope, cancer, and low baseline cardiopulmonary reserve are the drivers; PESI/sPESI perform well precisely because they are mostly comorbidity plus hemodynamics. [2,4]
Bleeding is a competing outcome you own: intracranial hemorrhage after full-dose systemic lysis runs about 2%, with a steep rise in age >75. Weigh this explicitly rather than reflexively. [3]

Longer-term: about half of PE survivors report persistent dyspnea or exercise limitation (post-PE syndrome), and roughly 0.5–4% develop chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). Symptomatic patients at 3–6 months need echo — and if PH is present, referral for right heart catheterization and V/Q scanning, since pulmonary endarterectomy is potentially curative. [1,2]
Recurrence after stopping anticoagulation for unprovoked PE is roughly 10% at 1 year and 30% at 5 years — the number that justifies indefinite reduced-dose DOAC therapy. [7]
sections.teaching_pearl: Every PE patient needs a 3–6 month follow-up visit that asks one question: are you back to your baseline exertional capacity? That single question is how CTEPH gets diagnosed before the RV fails again.

summary_points: PE kills via the right ventricle: acute afterload → RV dilation → rising wall tension with falling coronary perfusion → RV ischemia → septal shift → loss of LV preload and cardiac output. Every risk tool is a surrogate for where the patient sits on that spiral.

The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline is the US reference and RETIRES 'massive/submassive' in favor of clinical categories A–E; ESC 2019 remains European standard with low / intermediate-low / intermediate-high / high. State which taxonomy you are using. [1,2]

Stratify with four inputs: hemodynamics, sPESI (0 = low risk, ~1% 30-day mortality), RV dysfunction on echo or CT (RV/LV ≥0.9–1.0), and troponin. Intermediate-high = stable BUT both RV dysfunction and positive troponin. [1,2,4]

High risk (shock/arrest) gets systemic alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours; intermediate-high gets anticoagulation plus 48–72 hours of monitoring with a written rescue-lysis plan — PEITHO showed up-front lysis reduces decompensation but causes ~2% ICH with no mortality benefit. [1,3]

Low risk with sPESI 0, no RV dysfunction, and adequate support can go home on a single-drug DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban); dabigatran and edoxaban need a parenteral lead-in. Treat at least 3 months, then decide provoked vs unprovoked. [1,5,7]
Two pitfalls: fluid-loading the hypotensive PE patient (use norepinephrine instead), and grading severity by clot size on the CT report instead of by RV size and troponin.
Follow survivors at 3–6 months — post-PE syndrome affects roughly half, and 0.5–4% develop CTEPH, which is potentially curable with pulmonary endarterectomy. [1,2]

gemini_errors: Defines intermediate-high risk as RV dysfunction plus 'troponin OR BNP'; ESC 2019 specifically requires elevated cardiac troponin (natriuretic peptides are not part of the ESC intermediate-high definition).

Asserts specific letter mapping ('PE + hypotension = high-risk/Category E') as fact; the letter-to-severity mapping of the new AHA/ACC categories is stated with more certainty than the source supports.

Extended-phase claim ('low-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BID or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily ... per AMPLIFY-EXT/EINSTEIN-CHOICE') is cited to refs 6 and 7, which are AMPLIFY (acute treatment) and EINSTEIN-PE (acute treatment) — trials that do not support reduced-dose extended therapy; citation mismatch.
McConnell sign presented as distinguishing acute PE from chronic RV pressure overload; it is neither sensitive nor specific (also seen in RV infarction) and should not be used as a discriminator.
HoT-PE mis-cited to Eur Respir J; it was published in Eur Heart J 2020;41:509.
'Low-risk PE (sPESI 0) carries under 1% 30-day mortality' — validation data show ~1.0–1.1%, so this understates it slightly.
claude_errors: PEITHO figures slightly conflated: 5.6% vs 2.6% was the composite primary endpoint (death OR hemodynamic decompensation) at 7 days, not hemodynamic decompensation alone (1.6% vs 5.0%); repeated in the Outcomes section as 'placebo-arm hemodynamic collapse was 5.6%'.
Quoted 5–15% mortality for intermediate-high-risk PE is at the high end/overstated; ESC-cited and PEITHO-derived 30-day mortality for this group is generally ~2–10%.
judge.why: Both share the same core physiology framework and both handle the taxonomy question responsibly (2026 AHA/ACC categories vs ESC 2019 four-tier, massive/submassive retired). A is more precise where it counts: correct sPESI items, correct ESC operational definitions of all four strata, accurate PEITHO numbers (1006 patients, 6.3% vs 1.2% major extracranial bleeding, ~2% ICH), accurate HoT-PE recurrence rate and journal, correct YEARS thresholds, and it adds high-yield management content B omits (norepinephrine rather than volume loading, cancer-associated VTE, APS/CrCl<30 exceptions, CTEPH/post-PE syndrome follow-up). A is also appropriately hedged about catheter-directed therapy and about which letter category equals shock. B contains a genuine citation-honesty problem (extended-therapy claim attributed to AMPLIFY and EINSTEIN-PE, which do not support it), loosens the ESC intermediate-high definition to include BNP, overstates McConnell's discriminatory value, and mis-cites HoT-PE's journal. Teaching value and citation fidelity both favor A.

question.stem:
A 58-year-old woman is evaluated in the emergency department for pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that began 6 hours ago after a 10-hour flight. She has no cancer or prior VTE. She takes no medications and is otherwise healthy.

Temperature 37.0 C, BP 118/76 mm Hg, HR 96/min, RR 20/min, SpO2 94% on room air. She is comfortable at rest, mildly tachypneic; no jugular venous distension or peripheral edema.

CT pulmonary angiogram confirms bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli. Troponin I is 0.09 ng/mL (upper limit 0.04). Transthoracic echo shows RV dilation with a flattened interventricular septum and mildly reduced RV systolic function; LV function is normal. sPESI score is 0.
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Admit for anticoagulation and hemodynamic monitoring

question.explanation: This patient is hemodynamically stable (normal BP, no shock) but has both RV dysfunction on echo AND biomarker elevation (troponin), placing her in the intermediate-high risk category (ESC 2019 taxonomy) / an acute PE clinical category with adverse prognostic markers but preserved hemodynamics (2026 AHA/ACC guideline, which retires the massive/submassive vocabulary in favor of Category A-E). Per this guideline, intermediate-high risk patients should be admitted for therapeutic anticoagulation and monitored for 48-72 hours, with rescue systemic thrombolysis reserved only if hemodynamic decompensation develops. The PEITHO trial demonstrated that routine systemic thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE reduces hemodynamic decompensation but significantly increases major and intracranial hemorrhage without a mortality benefit, so it is not given empirically when the patient is stable. Her sPESI of 0 reflects low 30-day mortality risk by clinical variables alone, but sPESI does not incorporate RV imaging or biomarkers, and the guideline mandates escalating risk assessment beyond sPESI when RV strain is present. Outpatient management is therefore inappropriate despite the reassuring sPESI. Catheter-directed therapy is evolving (ULTIMA, PE-TRACT) but is not first-line in a stable patient without decompensation.

wrong_explanations.why: Catheter-directed thrombolysis is being studied (ULTIMA, PE-TRACT) but is not indicated as initial therapy in a hemodynamically stable patient; it is reserved for those who deteriorate or when systemic lysis is contraindicated in high-risk PE.
IVC filters are reserved for patients with a contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrent VTE despite adequate anticoagulation, neither of which applies here.

An sPESI of 0 alone suggests low-risk, but RV dysfunction plus troponin elevation upgrades her to intermediate-high risk, which requires inpatient monitoring, not outpatient DOAC therapy (HoT-PE criteria are not met).

Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk PE with shock or hemodynamic instability; per PEITHO, using it empirically in a stable intermediate-risk patient increases major bleeding without a mortality benefit.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must integrate hemodynamic stability, sPESI, troponin, and RV imaging simultaneously to correctly place the patient into the intermediate-high risk tier and reject both an undertreatment (outpatient DOAC) and overtreatment (systemic thrombolysis) trap.
reasoning_steps: Recognize hemodynamic stability (normal BP, no shock) rules out high-risk PE and empiric systemic thrombolysis
Calculate sPESI = 0, suggesting low clinical risk by symptoms/vitals alone
Recognize that RV dysfunction on echo plus elevated troponin reclassifies her as intermediate-high risk despite the low sPESI
Apply 2026 AHA/ACC/ESC 2019 risk-adapted management: intermediate-high risk requires inpatient anticoagulation with monitoring, reserving thrombolysis for decompensation
Exclude catheter-directed lysis and IVC filter as premature/inappropriate given her current stability

talk.key_point: In intermediate-high risk PE (RV dysfunction plus positive biomarkers but hemodynamically stable), the correct initial strategy is inpatient anticoagulation with close monitoring, reserving thrombolysis for hemodynamic decompensation.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Acute Pulmonary Embolism: Risk Stratification and Management

board_pearls: Mechanism: RV dysfunction from acute pressure overload plus myocardial troponin release identifies patients at higher risk of hemodynamic collapse even when systemic BP remains normal.

2026 AHA/ACC guideline replaces massive/submassive terminology with acute PE Clinical Categories A-E and recommends 48-72h monitoring with rescue lysis only on decompensation for intermediate-high risk PE.
Discriminator versus low-risk PE: sPESI of 0 alone is insufficient to exclude intermediate-high risk if echo shows RV strain or troponin is elevated — both must be checked.

PEITHO trial: routine systemic thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE reduced decompensation but significantly increased major and intracranial hemorrhage, establishing thrombolysis as reserved for high-risk/decompensating patients only [3].

Common trap: treating a low sPESI as sufficient for outpatient DOAC therapy without incorporating RV imaging/biomarker data, or overtreating a stable intermediate-risk patient with empiric thrombolysis.
teaching_points: PE risk stratification requires integrating hemodynamics, clinical scores (sPESI), RV imaging, and cardiac biomarkers — no single tool is sufficient alone.

The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline is the first dedicated US PE guideline and introduces acute PE Clinical Categories A-E, retiring massive/submassive terminology; ESC 2019 remains the parallel low/intermediate-low/intermediate-high/high taxonomy.
Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk (shock) PE or intermediate-high risk patients who decompensate during monitoring, not given empirically to stable patients with RV strain alone.
summary_points: Hemodynamically stable PE with RV dysfunction AND troponin elevation = intermediate-high risk; manage with anticoagulation plus 48-72h monitoring, not empiric thrombolysis.

question.stem:
A 71-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department for 3 days of progressive dyspnea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has not had syncope, hemoptysis, or leg pain. He takes no medications, has had no recent surgery or trauma, and has no history of cancer or bleeding.

Temperature 37.1 C, BP 116/74 mm Hg, HR 112/min, RR 24/min, SpO2 91% on room air. He is alert with warm extremities. There is jugular venous distention and a loud P2; lungs are clear.

Troponin I 0.14 ng/mL (reference <0.04), BNP 640 pg/mL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, lactate 1.5 mmol/L. CT pulmonary angiography shows bilateral lobar filling defects with an RV/LV diameter ratio of 1.3. Bedside echocardiography demonstrates RV dilatation with hypokinesis and preserved LV function.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Administer systemic alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours
Begin apixaban and discharge with outpatient follow-up
Initiate unfractionated heparin with continuous monitoring
Insert a retrievable inferior vena cava filter

question.explanation: This patient is normotensive (BP 116/74) but has BOTH RV dysfunction (RV/LV 1.3, echo hypokinesis) AND myocardial injury (troponin 0.14), with sPESI >=1 (HR >110). That defines intermediate-HIGH risk PE in the ESC 2019 four-strata scheme, and a non-high-risk category with RV dysfunction plus biomarker elevation in the 2026 AHA/ACC clinical categories A-E taxonomy (which formally retires the terms massive and submassive). Both documents recommend the same pathway: prompt therapeutic parenteral anticoagulation (weight-based UFH is preferred over LMWH when advanced therapy might be needed on short notice) and admission to a monitored setting for 48-72 hours, with reperfusion held in reserve as RESCUE therapy if hemodynamic decompensation occurs [1,2]. The critical discriminator is the absence of shock: there is no hypotension, no vasopressor requirement, normal lactate, and warm extremities. PEITHO validated exactly this strategy - upfront tenecteplase in intermediate-risk PE reduced hemodynamic decompensation but caused a significant excess of major bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage with no mortality benefit, so routine primary systemic lysis in normotensive patients is not recommended [3]. Escalation should be driven by trajectory (worsening tachycardia, hypotension, rising lactate/oxygen requirement) rather than by the initial imaging and biomarker profile alone. Activation of a PE response team, where available, is reasonable to plan contingency reperfusion [1].

wrong_explanations.why: Full-dose systemic thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk PE with shock, persistent hypotension, or cardiac arrest. This patient is hemodynamically stable; PEITHO showed upfront lysis in intermediate-risk PE increases major and intracranial bleeding without a mortality benefit [3].
Outpatient single-drug DOAC therapy (HoT-PE) applies only to low-risk PE with sPESI 0 and no RV dysfunction. Elevated troponin, RV/LV 1.3, hypokinesis, and HR 112 exclude home management [4].

IVC filters are indicated only when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated or fails despite therapeutic dosing. This patient has no bleeding contraindication, and filters do not treat existing RV strain or reduce mortality.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis is an evolving option (ULTIMA improved RV/LV ratio; PE-TRACT ongoing) and is best used as rescue therapy or when systemic lysis is contraindicated - not as the initial step in a stable intermediate-high risk patient [1,5].

question.difficulty_rationale: The item requires assembling four separate data streams (hemodynamics, sPESI, RV imaging, troponin) into a specific risk stratum, then recognizing that this stratum mandates surveillance with rescue reperfusion rather than any upfront reperfusion modality; two reperfusion distractors are genuinely attractive.
reasoning_steps: Confirm hemodynamic status: normotensive with normal lactate and warm extremities, so this is NOT high-risk (no shock).
Identify markers of RV compromise: RV/LV ratio 1.3 with echo hypokinesis PLUS troponin elevation, and sPESI >=1 from HR 112.
Assign the stratum: normotension + RV dysfunction + positive biomarker = intermediate-high risk (ESC 2019) / non-high-risk with RV dysfunction and injury (2026 AHA/ACC categories).
Apply the guideline pathway for that stratum: therapeutic parenteral anticoagulation (UFH preferred for potential escalation) plus 48-72 hours of monitoring, reperfusion reserved as rescue.

Eliminate reperfusion and disposition errors: upfront systemic lysis (PEITHO bleeding excess), upfront CDT (unproven as first-line), home DOAC (sPESI/RV criteria not met), and IVC filter (no anticoagulation contraindication).

talk.key_point: In normotensive acute PE with both RV dysfunction and elevated troponin (intermediate-high risk), give therapeutic parenteral anticoagulation and monitor 48-72 hours, reserving thrombolysis for hemodynamic decompensation [1,2].

abim_classification.specific_topic: Acute PE risk stratification: intermediate-high risk management

board_pearls: The mechanism of intermediate-high risk PE is acute RV pressure overload: RV dilatation (RV/LV >=0.9-1.0) causes ischemic microinjury with troponin release before systemic hypotension appears, which is why imaging plus biomarker positivity identifies patients at risk of later decompensation.

The 2026 AHA/ACC PE guideline is the first dedicated US PE document and replaces massive/submassive with clinical categories A-E; ESC 2019 remains current in Europe with low / intermediate-low / intermediate-high / high strata - always state which taxonomy you are using [1,2].

The single discriminator between systemic thrombolysis and anticoagulation-plus-monitoring is hemodynamics, not the troponin or the RV/LV ratio: shock, persistent hypotension, or arrest, not RV strain alone, triggers primary reperfusion [1,2].

PEITHO (NEJM 2014) randomized normotensive intermediate-risk PE to tenecteplase: hemodynamic decompensation fell but major bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage rose significantly with no mortality benefit - the basis for the rescue-only strategy [3].

The most common trap is treating a positive troponin plus RV dilatation as an automatic indication to lyse; the correct response is escalation readiness (UFH, monitored bed, PE response team) with lysis only if the patient decompensates.
teaching_points: Risk-stratify every acute PE using four elements in sequence: hemodynamics, sPESI (or PESI), RV size/function on CT or echo, and cardiac troponin.
Low-risk PE with sPESI 0 and no RV dysfunction can be treated at home with a single-drug DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban); dabigatran and edoxaban require a parenteral lead-in [4,6].
Unfractionated heparin is preferred over LMWH when reperfusion may be needed imminently, given its short half-life and reversibility; anticoagulate for at least 3 months in all patients [1,6].
summary_points: Normotensive PE with RV dysfunction plus troponin elevation = intermediate-high risk: anticoagulate, monitor 48-72 hours, and lyse only as rescue [1,2,3].

visual_memory_card.bottom_left: Intermediate-high: heparin, monitor, rescue lysis
visual_memory_card.bottom_right: Positive troponin alone does not justify lysis

gemini_errors: Core classification error: a patient with sPESI 0 who has RV dysfunction and elevated troponin is classified as 'intermediate-HIGH risk.' ESC 2019 explicitly states that patients in PESI class I–II or with sPESI 0 who have elevated biomarkers and/or RV dysfunction on imaging are classified as INTERMEDIATE-LOW risk; intermediate-high requires PESI III–V or sPESI ≥1 PLUS both RV dysfunction and positive troponin.

Reasoning step 'RV dysfunction on echo plus elevated troponin reclassifies her as intermediate-high risk despite the low sPESI' is a direct misstatement of the ESC 2019 algorithm and is attributed to that guideline.
Overstated strength: says the guideline 'mandates escalating risk assessment beyond sPESI' — no cited document uses mandatory language.
Same unverifiable '2026 AHA/ACC Categories A–E' attribution with specific recommendations.
claude_errors: Both artifacts cite a '2026 AHA/ACC Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guideline' with 'Clinical Categories A–E' as an established, citable document with specific recommendations (48–72 h monitoring, rescue-only lysis); this attribution/level of specificity cannot be verified and risks fabricated guideline sourcing.
ABIM blueprint weight for Pulmonary Disease listed as '10%' is an approximation (published weight is ~9%) — trivial.
judge.why: Both items converge on the same defensible management answer (parenteral anticoagulation plus monitored bed, rescue lysis only for decompensation) and both cite PEITHO correctly. The decisive difference is guideline fidelity: Artifact B constructs a vignette with sPESI 0 and then labels it intermediate-HIGH risk, which directly contradicts the ESC 2019 stratification it cites (sPESI 0 with RV dysfunction/positive troponin = intermediate-LOW). That error is not incidental — it is the teaching point of the item and would actively miseducate a resident on the exact table boards test. Artifact A builds a clean intermediate-high vignette (HR 112 → sPESI ≥1, RV/LV 1.3, troponin+), correctly states the ESC criteria, correctly frames UFH preference for possible escalation, accurately summarizes PEITHO (reduced decompensation, excess major/intracranial bleeding, no mortality benefit), correctly limits HoT-PE to sPESI 0 without RV dysfunction, and correctly notes dabigatran/edoxaban require parenteral lead-in. Both share the same unverifiable '2026 AHA/ACC' citation, so that concern is a wash. A is superior on accuracy, guideline fidelity, and teaching value.

Timing of Initiation of Renal-Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury (STARRT-AKI)","year":2020,"society":"NEJM","type":"trial","url":"https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2000741"},{"id":4,"source":"Semler MW, et al. Balanced Crystalloids versus Saline in Critically Ill Adults (SMART)","year":2018,"society":"NEJM","type":"trial","url":"https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1711584"}],"sections":[{"heading":"Physiology First: How GFR Is Actually Maintained","minutes":"2-3 min","points":["GFR = Kf x (Pgc - Pbs - πgc). The glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pgc) that drives filtration is a function of the balance between afferent and efferent arteriolar tone, not a fixed number.","During systemic hypoperfusion, the kidney defends GFR via two reflexes: afferent arteriolar vasodilation (mediated by prostaglandins, especially PGE2/PGI2) and efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction (mediated by angiotensin II). This preserves Pgc even as renal blood flow falls.","This is exactly why NSAIDs (block afferent dilation via COX inhibition) and ACEi/ARB (block efferent constriction) can precipitate a sharp GFR drop in a volume-down or renal-artery-stenotic patient - the compensatory mechanism is pharmacologically disabled.","The proximal tubule (S3 segment) and thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle live in the renal medulla, an area of physiologically low oxygen tension (~10-20 mmHg) because of countercurrent exchange - they are maximally vulnerable to any further drop in perfusion."],"teaching_pearl":"Think of prerenal physiology as a 'hemodynamic' problem the kidney is actively compensating for - NSAIDs and RAS blockers don't cause AKI, they remove the kidney's own compensation.","board_tip":"A classic board vignette: patient on an ACEi + NSAID + diuretic ('triple whammy') develops AKI after a diarrheal illness - test is asking you to recognize loss of autoregulatory reserve, not primary nephrotoxicity."},{"heading":"Pathophysiology: Prerenal Azotemia to Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)","minutes":"2-3 min","points":["If hypoperfusion is severe or prolonged enough that autoregulation fails, medullary tubular cells become ATP-depleted. Loss of ATP disrupts the actin cytoskeleton, causing loss of tight junction integrity, cell polarity, and eventual detachment of viable and necrotic tubular epithelial cells into the lumen.","Sloughed cells and debris form casts that obstruct the tubule lumen, raising intratubular pressure and directly reducing net filtration pressure (Pbs rises).","Disrupted tight junctions allow 'backleak' of filtrate from the tubular lumen into the interstitium, further lowering effective GFR independent of any hemodynamic change.","Increased distal NaCl delivery (because injured proximal tubule can't reabsorb normally) is sensed by the macula densa, triggering tubuloglomerular feedback - afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction - which paradoxically worsens perfusion in a feed-forward loop.","Nephrotoxic ATN follows a parallel but distinct route: aminoglycosides are taken up by megalin-mediated endocytosis in proximal tubule cells and accumulate to toxic concentrations; iodinated contrast causes direct tubular oxidative injury plus medullary vasoconstriction, compounding ischemic vulnerability."],"mechanism":"ATN is not a single hit but a self-amplifying cycle: ischemia -> tubular cell death -> luminal obstruction + backleak -> reduced GFR -> macula densa-driven vasoconstriction -> more ischemia. This is why removing the inciting nephrotoxin or restoring perfusion does not immediately reverse injury - the tubular epithelium must regenerate.","teaching_pearl":"Muddy brown granular casts on urine microscopy are literally the sloughed, necrotic tubular epithelial debris described above - the histology is on your urine dipstick.","board_tip":"Distinguish prerenal azotemia (intact tubular concentrating function, FeNa <1%) from ATN (tubular dysfunction, FeNa >2%) - but remember FeNa is unreliable if the patient is on diuretics; use FeUrea (<35%) instead in that setting."},{"heading":"Staging, Localizing, and Working Up AKI","minutes":"2 min","points":["KDIGO 2012 stages AKI by serum creatinine and urine output, not etiology: Stage 1 = Cr 1.5-1.9x baseline or ≥0.3 mg/dL rise in 48h, or UOP <0.5 mL/kg/h x 6-12h. Stage 2 = Cr 2.0-2.9x baseline, UOP <0.5 mL/kg/h x ≥12h. Stage 3 = Cr ≥3x baseline, Cr ≥4.0 mg/dL, RRT initiation, or UOP <0.3 mL/kg/h x ≥24h/anuria x12h [1].","Bucket the etiology into prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal - this determines the entire management pathway [1].","Renal US is mandatory early to exclude obstruction (postrenal) - hydronephrosis may be absent early or in retroperitoneal encasement, so a normal US doesn't fully exclude obstruction if suspicion is high.","Urine microscopy localizes intrinsic disease: muddy brown granular casts (ATN), white cell casts + eosinophils (acute interstitial nephritis), dysmorphic RBCs/RBC casts (glomerulonephritis).","History should specifically screen for nephrotoxin exposure (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, ACEi/ARB, vancomycin) and volume status (orthostatics, JVP, skin turgor, recent GI losses)."],"teaching_pearl":"Staging by KDIGO criteria isn't academic - stage correlates directly with in-hospital mortality and need for RRT, so it belongs in every AKI note.","board_tip":"A rising creatinine with a bland urine sediment and history of hypotension = prerenal or early ATN; add casts and it's established ATN; add eosinophils/rash/new drug = AIN - the exam wants you to sequence the story."},{"heading":"Management per KDIGO 2012: Supportive Care and RRT Timing","minutes":"2-3 min","points":["Treat the bucket: optimize volume/perfusion for prerenal physiology, relieve obstruction (Foley, nephrostomy) for postrenal, and for intrinsic disease remove the offending nephrotoxin and treat the underlying cause (e.g., steroids for AIN, immunosuppression for GN) [1].","Hold nephrotoxins - NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, avoid unnecessary contrast - because these agents directly impair the compensatory afferent/efferent tone or cause proximal tubular toxicity described above [1].","Use balanced crystalloids over normal saline for volume resuscitation when fluids are indicated; large-volume 0.9% saline causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and renal vasoconstriction that can worsen AKI risk - trial evidence from SMART supports this preference in critically ill patients [4].","Low-dose 'renal-dose' dopamine has no proven benefit and is not recommended [1].","RRT indications follow the classic AEIOU framework: refractory Acidosis, refractory hyperkalemia (Electrolytes), dialyzable Ingestions (lithium, salicylates, toxic alcohols), refractory volume Overload, and Uremic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis, uremic bleeding) [1].","Timing: KDIGO 2012 and subsequent landmark trials support a watchful-waiting/standard strategy rather than early/accelerated RRT initiation - AKIKI showed no mortality benefit to early RRT and more catheter-related complications with early initiation [2]; STARRT-AKI confirmed no benefit to an accelerated strategy across a broader critically ill population and showed higher rates of RRT dependence and adverse events with early initiation [3]."],"mechanism":"RRT corrects the acute biochemical derangements (K+, acid-base, volume) that threaten life, but it does not accelerate tubular epithelial regeneration - the kidney recovers on its own timeline. This is exactly why trials find no mortality benefit to earlier initiation absent a hard indication: RRT is bridging therapy, not disease-modifying therapy.","teaching_pearl":"AKIKI and STARRT-AKI together support a strategy of treating the specific derangement, not the number - don't dialyze for a creatinine value alone.","board_tip":"Board question pattern: patient with AKI, K+ 6.2 with peaked T waves and no ECG changes responding to medical therapy - answer is medical management (insulin/dextrose, calcium gluconate stabilization), not emergent dialysis, unless refractory."},{"heading":"Outcomes & Prognosis","minutes":"1-2 min","points":["AKI severity by KDIGO stage tracks directly with mortality; critically ill patients with Stage 3 AKI requiring RRT carry in-hospital mortality often cited in the 40-60% range depending on comorbidity burden and underlying critical illness [1].","A substantial fraction of AKI survivors, particularly those with more severe or prolonged injury, transition to CKD - the 'AKI-to-CKD continuum' is now a recognized entity, and even patients who appear to 'fully recover' creatinine warrant longer-term nephrology follow-up.","Recovery of native kidney function is the rule for most survivors of ATN, but dialysis dependence at 90 days is a meaningful minority outcome, especially with more severe AKI stage or delayed recovery.","The strongest prognostic drivers are the underlying critical illness (sepsis, cardiogenic shock) rather than the AKI itself in isolation - AKI is often a marker of illness severity as much as an independent mortality driver."],"teaching_pearl":"Every patient discharged after an AKI episode - even with a creatinine that returns to baseline - should have a follow-up eGFR checked, because subclinical nephron loss from that episode raises long-term CKD risk.","board_tip":"Know that a 2026 KDIGO AKI guideline update is currently in review - expect refinement of biomarker use and RRT criteria, but the AEIOU/staged framework taught here remains the current standard [1]."}],"summary_points":["GFR during hypoperfusion is defended by afferent vasodilation (prostaglandins) and efferent vasoconstriction (angiotensin II) - NSAIDs and ACEi/ARB remove these compensations and can precipitate AKI, especially in combination ('triple whammy') [1].","ATN is a self-amplifying cycle of tubular cell death, luminal obstruction, backleak, and tubuloglomerular feedback-mediated vasoconstriction - this explains why recovery takes time even after the inciting insult is removed.","KDIGO 2012 stages AKI by creatinine rise and urine output; bucket every case into prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal to guide management [1].","RRT is indicated for refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, dialyzable ingestions, volume overload, or uremia (AEIOU) - not for a creatinine number alone [1].","AKIKI and STARRT-AKI both showed no mortality benefit to early/accelerated RRT initiation over a watchful-waiting strategy, and early initiation increased catheter-related complications and RRT dependence [2,3].","AKI severity predicts both short-term mortality and long-term CKD risk - all AKI survivors deserve follow-up renal function testing."],"visual_memory_card":{"top_left":"Ischemia/toxin depletes ATP, disrupts tubular cell tight junctions","top_right":"Rising Cr/BUN, oliguria, muddy brown casts, hyperkalemia","bottom_left":"KDIGO stage + urine microscopy + renal US to localize cause","bottom_right":"Fix perfusion/obstruction, hold nephrotoxins, RRT only for AEIOU"}}
