sections.heading: Physiology First: How GFR Is Actually Maintained
points: GFR = Kf x (Pgc - Pbs - πgc). The glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pgc) that drives filtration is a function of the balance between afferent and efferent arteriolar tone, not a fixed number.

During systemic hypoperfusion, the kidney defends GFR via two reflexes: afferent arteriolar vasodilation (mediated by prostaglandins, especially PGE2/PGI2) and efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction (mediated by angiotensin II). This preserves Pgc even as renal blood flow falls.

This is exactly why NSAIDs (block afferent dilation via COX inhibition) and ACEi/ARB (block efferent constriction) can precipitate a sharp GFR drop in a volume-down or renal-artery-stenotic patient - the compensatory mechanism is pharmacologically disabled.

The proximal tubule (S3 segment) and thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle live in the renal medulla, an area of physiologically low oxygen tension (~10-20 mmHg) because of countercurrent exchange - they are maximally vulnerable to any further drop in perfusion.
sections.teaching_pearl: Think of prerenal physiology as a 'hemodynamic' problem the kidney is actively compensating for - NSAIDs and RAS blockers don't cause AKI, they remove the kidney's own compensation.
sections.board_tip: A classic board vignette: patient on an ACEi + NSAID + diuretic ('triple whammy') develops AKI after a diarrheal illness - test is asking you to recognize loss of autoregulatory reserve, not primary nephrotoxicity.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology: Prerenal Azotemia to Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)
points: If hypoperfusion is severe or prolonged enough that autoregulation fails, medullary tubular cells become ATP-depleted. Loss of ATP disrupts the actin cytoskeleton, causing loss of tight junction integrity, cell polarity, and eventual detachment of viable and necrotic tubular epithelial cells into the lumen.
Sloughed cells and debris form casts that obstruct the tubule lumen, raising intratubular pressure and directly reducing net filtration pressure (Pbs rises).
Disrupted tight junctions allow 'backleak' of filtrate from the tubular lumen into the interstitium, further lowering effective GFR independent of any hemodynamic change.

Increased distal NaCl delivery (because injured proximal tubule can't reabsorb normally) is sensed by the macula densa, triggering tubuloglomerular feedback - afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction - which paradoxically worsens perfusion in a feed-forward loop.

Nephrotoxic ATN follows a parallel but distinct route: aminoglycosides are taken up by megalin-mediated endocytosis in proximal tubule cells and accumulate to toxic concentrations; iodinated contrast causes direct tubular oxidative injury plus medullary vasoconstriction, compounding ischemic vulnerability.
sections.mechanism: ATN is not a single hit but a self-amplifying cycle: ischemia -> tubular cell death -> luminal obstruction + backleak -> reduced GFR -> macula densa-driven vasoconstriction -> more ischemia. This is why removing the inciting nephrotoxin or restoring perfusion does not immediately reverse injury - the tubular epithelium must regenerate.
sections.teaching_pearl: Muddy brown granular casts on urine microscopy are literally the sloughed, necrotic tubular epithelial debris described above - the histology is on your urine dipstick.
sections.board_tip: Distinguish prerenal azotemia (intact tubular concentrating function, FeNa <1%) from ATN (tubular dysfunction, FeNa >2%) - but remember FeNa is unreliable if the patient is on diuretics; use FeUrea (<35%) instead in that setting.

sections.heading: Staging, Localizing, and Working Up AKI
points: KDIGO 2012 stages AKI by serum creatinine and urine output, not etiology: Stage 1 = Cr 1.5-1.9x baseline or ≥0.3 mg/dL rise in 48h, or UOP <0.5 mL/kg/h x 6-12h. Stage 2 = Cr 2.0-2.9x baseline, UOP <0.5 mL/kg/h x ≥12h. Stage 3 = Cr ≥3x baseline, Cr ≥4.0 mg/dL, RRT initiation, or UOP <0.3 mL/kg/h x ≥24h/anuria x12h [1].
Bucket the etiology into prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal - this determines the entire management pathway [1].

Renal US is mandatory early to exclude obstruction (postrenal) - hydronephrosis may be absent early or in retroperitoneal encasement, so a normal US doesn't fully exclude obstruction if suspicion is high.
Urine microscopy localizes intrinsic disease: muddy brown granular casts (ATN), white cell casts + eosinophils (acute interstitial nephritis), dysmorphic RBCs/RBC casts (glomerulonephritis).
History should specifically screen for nephrotoxin exposure (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, ACEi/ARB, vancomycin) and volume status (orthostatics, JVP, skin turgor, recent GI losses).
sections.teaching_pearl: Staging by KDIGO criteria isn't academic - stage correlates directly with in-hospital mortality and need for RRT, so it belongs in every AKI note.
sections.board_tip: A rising creatinine with a bland urine sediment and history of hypotension = prerenal or early ATN; add casts and it's established ATN; add eosinophils/rash/new drug = AIN - the exam wants you to sequence the story.

sections.heading: Management per KDIGO 2012: Supportive Care and RRT Timing
points: Treat the bucket: optimize volume/perfusion for prerenal physiology, relieve obstruction (Foley, nephrostomy) for postrenal, and for intrinsic disease remove the offending nephrotoxin and treat the underlying cause (e.g., steroids for AIN, immunosuppression for GN) [1].

Hold nephrotoxins - NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, avoid unnecessary contrast - because these agents directly impair the compensatory afferent/efferent tone or cause proximal tubular toxicity described above [1].

Use balanced crystalloids over normal saline for volume resuscitation when fluids are indicated; large-volume 0.9% saline causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and renal vasoconstriction that can worsen AKI risk - trial evidence from SMART supports this preference in critically ill patients [4].
Low-dose 'renal-dose' dopamine has no proven benefit and is not recommended [1].

RRT indications follow the classic AEIOU framework: refractory Acidosis, refractory hyperkalemia (Electrolytes), dialyzable Ingestions (lithium, salicylates, toxic alcohols), refractory volume Overload, and Uremic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis, uremic bleeding) [1].

Timing: KDIGO 2012 and subsequent landmark trials support a watchful-waiting/standard strategy rather than early/accelerated RRT initiation - AKIKI showed no mortality benefit to early RRT and more catheter-related complications with early initiation [2]; STARRT-AKI confirmed no benefit to an accelerated strategy across a broader critically ill population and showed higher rates of RRT dependence and adverse events with early initiation [3].
sections.mechanism: RRT corrects the acute biochemical derangements (K+, acid-base, volume) that threaten life, but it does not accelerate tubular epithelial regeneration - the kidney recovers on its own timeline. This is exactly why trials find no mortality benefit to earlier initiation absent a hard indication: RRT is bridging therapy, not disease-modifying therapy.
sections.teaching_pearl: AKIKI and STARRT-AKI together support a strategy of treating the specific derangement, not the number - don't dialyze for a creatinine value alone.
sections.board_tip: Board question pattern: patient with AKI, K+ 6.2 with peaked T waves and no ECG changes responding to medical therapy - answer is medical management (insulin/dextrose, calcium gluconate stabilization), not emergent dialysis, unless refractory.

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: AKI severity by KDIGO stage tracks directly with mortality; critically ill patients with Stage 3 AKI requiring RRT carry in-hospital mortality often cited in the 40-60% range depending on comorbidity burden and underlying critical illness [1].

A substantial fraction of AKI survivors, particularly those with more severe or prolonged injury, transition to CKD - the 'AKI-to-CKD continuum' is now a recognized entity, and even patients who appear to 'fully recover' creatinine warrant longer-term nephrology follow-up.

Recovery of native kidney function is the rule for most survivors of ATN, but dialysis dependence at 90 days is a meaningful minority outcome, especially with more severe AKI stage or delayed recovery.

The strongest prognostic drivers are the underlying critical illness (sepsis, cardiogenic shock) rather than the AKI itself in isolation - AKI is often a marker of illness severity as much as an independent mortality driver.
sections.teaching_pearl: Every patient discharged after an AKI episode - even with a creatinine that returns to baseline - should have a follow-up eGFR checked, because subclinical nephron loss from that episode raises long-term CKD risk.
sections.board_tip: Know that a 2026 KDIGO AKI guideline update is currently in review - expect refinement of biomarker use and RRT criteria, but the AEIOU/staged framework taught here remains the current standard [1].

summary_points: GFR during hypoperfusion is defended by afferent vasodilation (prostaglandins) and efferent vasoconstriction (angiotensin II) - NSAIDs and ACEi/ARB remove these compensations and can precipitate AKI, especially in combination ('triple whammy') [1].

ATN is a self-amplifying cycle of tubular cell death, luminal obstruction, backleak, and tubuloglomerular feedback-mediated vasoconstriction - this explains why recovery takes time even after the inciting insult is removed.
KDIGO 2012 stages AKI by creatinine rise and urine output; bucket every case into prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal to guide management [1].
RRT is indicated for refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, dialyzable ingestions, volume overload, or uremia (AEIOU) - not for a creatinine number alone [1].

AKIKI and STARRT-AKI both showed no mortality benefit to early/accelerated RRT initiation over a watchful-waiting strategy, and early initiation increased catheter-related complications and RRT dependence [2,3].
AKI severity predicts both short-term mortality and long-term CKD risk - all AKI survivors deserve follow-up renal function testing.

sections.heading: Physiology: How the Glomerulus Defends GFR — and Exactly Where It Fails
points: GFR is a Starling filtration process: GFR = Kf x (glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure − Bowman pressure − plasma oncotic pressure). Only one of those terms is actively regulated minute-to-minute — glomerular capillary pressure — and it is set by the ratio of afferent to efferent arteriolar tone.

Afferent tone is relaxed by myogenic reflex and by vasodilatory prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) generated by COX-1/COX-2; efferent tone is raised by angiotensin II acting on AT1 receptors. This is why an NSAID (afferent constriction) plus an ACEi/ARB (efferent dilation) plus volume depletion is the classic 'triple whammy' that collapses filtration pressure.

Tubuloglomerular feedback: the macula densa senses distal NaCl via NKCC2; high delivery triggers adenosine release → A1-receptor afferent constriction, lowering GFR to protect tubular workload. This is a physiologic brake, not pathology, and it explains part of the eGFR dip seen after RASi or SGLT2i initiation.

Oxygen economics of the medulla: the outer medulla runs at a PO2 of roughly 10–20 mmHg because countercurrent vasa recta shunt oxygen while the S3 proximal segment and medullary thick ascending limb burn ATP on Na-K-ATPase. Any drop in perfusion hits these two segments first — hence 'ischemic ATN' is a medullary disease.

Cellular cascade of ATN: ATP depletion → Na-K-ATPase fails → cell swelling, loss of polarity, actin cytoskeletal breakdown → brush-border sloughing → three simultaneous injuries: (1) intratubular obstruction by casts, (2) transepithelial backleak of filtrate, (3) sustained afferent vasoconstriction from endothelial dysfunction and loss of nitric oxide. Filtration falls even when cardiac output is restored — this is why 'prerenal' physiology can persist as intrinsic injury after the insult resolves.

Sterile inflammation amplifies it: injured tubular cells release damage-associated molecular patterns activating TLR4, complement, and infiltrating monocytes/neutrophils; TNF and IL-6 worsen microvascular congestion. AKI is an inflammatory disease, not just a plumbing problem.

Definitions follow the physiology, not the other way around. KDIGO 2012: Cr rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, OR ≥1.5x baseline within 7 days, OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Stage 2 = 2x Cr; Stage 3 = 3x Cr, Cr ≥4.0 mg/dL, anuria ≥12 h, or need for RRT. [1]
sections.mechanism: Creatinine is a lagging, dilution-dependent marker of a hemodynamic and cellular process that is already hours old. Understanding afferent/efferent balance and medullary hypoxia lets you predict which drug or hemodynamic change caused a given Cr rise — and which reversible lever to pull.
sections.teaching_pearl: A Cr that rises 0.3–0.5 mg/dL over 48 h after starting an ACEi/ARB or SGLT2i is usually hemodynamic (efferent dilation or tubuloglomerular feedback), not injury — expect it, recheck, and do not reflexively stop the drug.
sections.board_tip: Creatinine kinetics matter: after a total ischemic insult, Cr rises only ~1–1.5 mg/dL per day, so a 'normal' Cr 6 hours into shock tells you nothing. Urine output and clinical context precede the number.

sections.heading: Three Buckets: Localizing the Lesion Because It Changes What You Do
points: KDIGO frames AKI in three etiologic buckets — prerenal (hemodynamic), intrinsic (tubular, interstitial, glomerular, vascular), and postrenal (obstruction) — precisely because each bucket has a different first action: restore perfusion, stop the toxin/treat the immune process, or decompress. [1]

Postrenal is cheapest to exclude and most reversible: bladder scan for post-void residual and renal US. Do it early in older men (benign prostatic hyperplasia), pelvic malignancy, retroperitoneal disease, or anuria. Obstruction relieved within days usually recovers; weeks of hydronephrosis leaves fibrosis.

Prerenal vs ATN — use the tubule as your assay. Intact tubules avidly reabsorb sodium under angiotensin II/aldosterone drive: fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) <1%, urine Na <20 mEq/L, bland sediment, high urine osmolality. Injured tubules cannot: FENa >2%, isosmotic urine, muddy-brown granular casts. Use fractional excretion of urea (<35% favors prerenal) if the patient is on a loop diuretic, because the loop forces natriuresis and invalidates FENa.

FENa lies in three classic settings: contrast nephropathy and rhabdomyolysis (intense vasoconstriction → low FENa despite tubular injury), and glomerulonephritis (tubules are intact, so FENa is low). Also low in hepatorenal syndrome and cardiorenal physiology.

Urine microscopy is the cheapest biopsy you have: muddy-brown casts = ATN; dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts = glomerulonephritis (send ANCA, anti-GBM, complements, ANA/dsDNA); white cell casts and eosinophiluria = acute interstitial nephritis (AIN, think PPI, NSAID, beta-lactam, checkpoint inhibitor); pigmented granular casts with heme-positive dipstick but no RBCs = myoglobinuria.

Do not forget the syndromes that need a specific answer today: rhabdomyolysis (CK, aggressive isotonic fluids), tumor lysis (uric acid, phosphate, LDH), cast nephropathy from myeloma (SPEP/free light chains, high anion-gap-normal setting), thrombotic microangiopathy (schistocytes, low platelets, high LDH), abdominal compartment syndrome, and cardiorenal/hepatorenal congestion (rising Cr with venous congestion, not arterial underfilling).

Baseline matters: compare to a real prior Cr, and after the episode restage kidney function — AKI is a defined risk factor for incident and progressive CKD and warrants eGFR and albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) follow-up in 3 months. [8]
sections.mechanism: FENa and urine sediment are direct readouts of tubular cell function: sodium avidity requires intact apical NHE3/NKCC2 and basolateral Na-K-ATPase, so its loss is a functional biomarker of the same ATP failure described in the physiology section.
sections.teaching_pearl: Venous congestion — not arterial underfilling — is a leading driver of AKI in decompensated HF and cirrhosis. Elevated renal venous pressure lowers the transrenal pressure gradient and raises interstitial pressure; here decongestion, not a fluid bolus, restores GFR.
sections.board_tip: Eosinophiluria is neither sensitive nor specific for AIN. A clean sediment with subnephrotic proteinuria, a suggestive drug exposure, and no other explanation is the more useful pattern; biopsy is the arbiter when steroids are being contemplated.

sections.heading: Management: Perfusion, Poisons, and When to Dialyze
points: The KDIGO 2012 core bundle is deceptively simple and still correct: stop nephrotoxins, optimize volume status and perfusion pressure, avoid hyperglycemia, avoid radiocontrast when avoidable, and monitor Cr and urine output. There is no drug that treats established ATN. [1]

Fluid: use balanced crystalloids preferentially. SMART (n≈15,800) showed a lower composite of death, new RRT, or persistent renal dysfunction with balanced crystalloid vs 0.9% saline (14.3% vs 15.4%), consistent with avoiding hyperchloremia-mediated afferent vasoconstriction; do not use hydroxyethyl starch, which increases AKI and death. Fluid is a drug with a therapeutic window — once the patient is congested, more fluid raises renal venous pressure and worsens GFR. [5]

Pressure: norepinephrine to restore mean arterial pressure (MAP) is not 'renal vasoconstriction' — it restores autoregulatory perfusion. SEPSISPAM found no overall mortality difference between MAP targets of 65–70 vs 80–85 mmHg, but in the prespecified chronic-hypertension subgroup the higher target reduced doubling of Cr and need for RRT — so individualize the target to the patient's usual pressure. [7]

Diuretics do not treat AKI. Loops (and mannitol, dopamine, natriuretic peptides) do not prevent AKI, hasten recovery, or reduce dialysis need; KDIGO recommends against using diuretics to prevent or treat AKI, reserving them for volume overload management. Converting oliguric to nonoliguric AKI is cosmetic. [1]

Contrast: the risk is real but far smaller than historically taught, and prophylaxis is minimal. PRESERVE (n=5,177, high-risk patients undergoing angiography) showed no benefit of sodium bicarbonate over isotonic saline and no benefit of N-acetylcysteine over placebo. Use isotonic volume expansion in high-risk patients, use the lowest necessary contrast volume, and do not withhold indicated imaging out of reflex. [6]

RRT timing: start for the classic indications — refractory hyperkalemia, refractory metabolic acidosis, refractory volume overload, uremic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding), and dialyzable intoxications. Do NOT start earlier merely because the Cr or stage is high. AKIKI and STARRT-AKI both showed no mortality benefit from accelerated initiation, and roughly 40–50% of the delayed-strategy patients never needed dialysis at all; STARRT-AKI found MORE persistent dialysis dependence at 90 days in the accelerated arm. [1,2,3]

But 'watchful waiting' has a floor: AKIKI-2 compared a delayed with a more-delayed strategy (waiting for BUN ~112 mg/dL or oliguria >72 h) and found no benefit and a signal toward higher mortality with further delay. Watch metabolics, not the clock. [4]

Drug stewardship is a therapeutic intervention: renally dose everything, hold NSAIDs, hold or reduce RASi in true hemodynamic AKI or shock — but per KDIGO 2021 do not abandon RASi long-term for a <30% eGFR decline or mild hyperkalemia; treat the potassium instead and resume the drug. Vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam carries an observed excess AKI signal — reconsider the combination when an alternative covers the syndrome. [9]
sections.mechanism: Every effective intervention in AKI works by restoring the terms of the Starling equation or removing an ongoing injury input: balanced fluid and vasopressors restore glomerular capillary pressure, decongestion lowers Bowman/interstitial pressure, and nephrotoxin withdrawal stops further ATP depletion in the S3 segment. Nothing accelerates tubular regeneration pharmacologically, which is why 'no drug treats ATN' is a mechanistic statement, not a nihilistic one.
sections.teaching_pearl: When you are tempted to start dialysis for a number, ask what physiologic derangement you are correcting. If you cannot name it (K, pH, volume, uremic symptom, toxin), the trials say you can safely wait — and about half of those patients will recover without ever being cannulated. [2,3]
sections.board_tip: KDIGO stage 3 AKI is not itself an indication for RRT. The board answer is the refractory-complication list. Conversely, AKIKI-2 is the counterweight: indefinite delay to extreme azotemia is not benign. [1,4]

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: AKI is common and prognostically loud: it complicates roughly 10–15% of all hospitalizations and up to ~50% of ICU admissions, and mortality scales stepwise with KDIGO stage independent of the inciting illness.

Dialysis-requiring AKI in critically ill patients carries in-hospital/90-day mortality in the range of 40–50% in the modern trial populations, and among survivors a substantial minority remain dialysis-dependent — in STARRT-AKI, dialysis dependence at 90 days was higher in the accelerated-initiation arm (10.4% vs 6.0%), a reminder that starting RRT is itself a prognostically consequential act. [2]

What drives prognosis is mostly not the kidney: it is the severity of the underlying illness (sepsis, shock, mechanical ventilation), number of failing organs, and comorbid baseline CKD. Oliguric AKI, need for RRT, and failure to recover by day 7–10 (acute kidney disease) all predict worse long-term outcomes.

Survivors are not cured. AKI substantially increases the risk of incident CKD, CKD progression, kidney failure, subsequent cardiovascular events, and recurrent AKI; the risk rises with severity, duration, and number of episodes.

Therefore the discharge plan is part of AKI care: document peak and discharge Cr, reconcile nephrotoxins and renally cleared drugs, decide deliberately about resuming RASi/SGLT2i, and recheck eGFR plus ACR at ~3 months to restage per KDIGO 2024 — with blood pressure managed to a standardized-office target (<130/80 per 2025 AHA/ACC; SBP <120 by standardized measurement per KDIGO 2021 in CKD when tolerated). [8,9,10]
sections.teaching_pearl: A large share of post-AKI patients are discharged without any documented kidney follow-up and without their held ACEi/ARB or statin ever restarted. The highest-yield outpatient intervention after AKI is a deliberate 3-month recheck with thoughtful re-initiation of guideline-indicated cardiorenal therapy. [8]
sections.board_tip: 'Recovered' creatinine does not mean recovered nephrons — up to half of functional reserve can be lost silently. New albuminuria after AKI is the marker that predicts progression.

summary_points: GFR is defended by the afferent/efferent tone ratio: prostaglandins dilate the afferent, angiotensin II constricts the efferent. NSAID + RASi + hypovolemia is the triple whammy that collapses filtration pressure.

The outer medulla (S3 proximal tubule, medullary thick ascending limb) lives at PO2 10–20 mmHg with the highest ATP demand, so ischemic ATN begins there; ATP failure produces cast obstruction, filtrate backleak, and persistent afferent vasoconstriction that outlast the original insult.

Localize before you treat: bladder scan/US for postrenal, FENa (or FEurea if on a loop) for prerenal vs ATN, and urine microscopy for the intrinsic subtype — muddy-brown casts (ATN), RBC casts (GN), WBC casts (AIN).

Treatment is perfusion and poison control: balanced crystalloids over saline (SMART), MAP restored with norepinephrine and individualized upward in chronic hypertension (SEPSISPAM), nephrotoxins held. Loop diuretics, dopamine, and mannitol do NOT treat or prevent AKI per KDIGO 2012. [1,5,7]

Dialyze for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, uremic complications, or a dialyzable toxin — not for a stage or a number. AKIKI and STARRT-AKI showed no benefit to accelerated initiation and more 90-day dialysis dependence with it; AKIKI-2 showed indefinite delay is also harmful. [1,2,3,4]

The commonest pitfall is treating the discharge creatinine as the end of the story: AKI survivors carry markedly higher risk of CKD, kidney failure, and cardiovascular events, so restage eGFR and ACR at ~3 months and deliberately resume indicated RASi/SGLT2i rather than leaving them off. [8,9]

gemini_errors: Board tip is internally contradictory and clinically wrong: 'K+ 6.2 with peaked T waves and no ECG changes' — peaked T waves ARE an ECG change of hyperkalemia, and their presence mandates urgent membrane stabilization/shifting, not reassurance
'Renal US is mandatory early' in all AKI overstates KDIGO 2012, which does not make universal imaging a strong recommendation
Teaches eosinophiluria/WBC casts as a discriminator for AIN without noting eosinophiluria's poor sensitivity/specificity — an outdated teaching point
Teaching pearl that 'NSAIDs and RAS blockers don't cause AKI' is an overstatement — NSAIDs also cause AIN and papillary necrosis, and both classes can cause true injury, not only unmasking
Attributes the claim that a 2026 KDIGO AKI update is in review to reference [1] (KDIGO 2012) — the cited source cannot support that statement
Attributes RRT-requiring AKI mortality of '40–60%' to KDIGO 2012 [1]; that figure derives from cohort/trial data rather than a guideline recommendation
claude_errors: States tubuloglomerular feedback 'explains part of the eGFR dip seen after RASi' — the RASi-induced dip is mediated by loss of angiotensin II–dependent efferent tone/reduced intraglomerular pressure, not TGF (TGF is the correct mechanism for SGLT2i)

'Afferent tone is relaxed by myogenic reflex' is loosely stated — the myogenic reflex constricts the afferent arteriole with rising perfusion pressure and relaxes it with falling pressure; as written it inverts the canonical description
Garbled/incorrect acid-base claim for myeloma cast nephropathy ('high anion-gap-normal setting'); myeloma with cationic paraprotein classically produces a low or normal anion gap
AKIKI-2 thresholds are imprecisely attributed: BUN ~112 mg/dL / oliguria >72 h defined the randomization (delayed) point, while the more-delayed arm waited to BUN ~140 mg/dL
judge.why: Both are pedagogically sound and physiology-first, but A is materially more accurate and more useful. A gets the trial evidence right with verifiable numbers (SMART MAKE30 14.3% vs 15.4%; STARRT-AKI 90-day dialysis dependence 10.4% vs 6.0%; PRESERVE n=5177 negative for bicarbonate and NAC; SEPSISPAM's chronic-hypertension renal subgroup), adds the essential counterweight of AKIKI-2 against indefinite delay, correctly states KDIGO's recommendation against diuretics/dopamine for prevention or treatment, and explicitly corrects common resident errors (FENa pitfalls in contrast/rhabdo/GN/HRS, eosinophiluria's poor test characteristics, venous congestion as a driver in cardiorenal/hepatorenal disease, post-AKI restaging with eGFR + ACR and deliberate RASi/SGLT2i resumption). Citations are honest and society/year-matched. B is accurate in its core physiology and staging and its ATN feed-forward cycle is well taught, but it is thinner (no contrast prophylaxis evidence, no diuretic-futility teaching, no post-AKI follow-up specifics), contains one clearly wrong board vignette (peaked T waves described as 'no ECG changes'), overstates ultrasound as mandatory, and commits two citation-fidelity lapses by hanging epidemiologic mortality figures and a claim about a future 2026 update on the 2012 KDIGO document. A's residual errors are minor mechanistic imprecisions rather than actionable clinical mistakes.

talk.title: Cardiac Surgery–Associated AKI: When to Start Dialysis
talk.subtitle: Distinguishing AKI severity from an emergent indication for renal replacement therapy
guideline_sources: KDIGO 2012 Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury

references.source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury
AKIKI Trial (Gaudry et al.)
STARRT-AKI Trial (Bagshaw et al.)

question.stem:
A 74-year-old man is evaluated on post-operative day 3 after CABG for decreased urine output. He has baseline CKD (creatinine 1.1 mg/dL) and received IV contrast for a pre-operative angiogram. His home lisinopril has been held. He is hemodynamically stable and has received adequate volume resuscitation intraoperatively and post-operatively.

Temperature 37.0 C, BP 118/70 mm Hg, HR 88/min, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air. No jugular venous distention, no crackles, no peripheral edema, no pericardial rub, alert and oriented.

Creatinine 3.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.1), BUN 68 mg/dL, potassium 5.3 mEq/L, bicarbonate 19 mEq/L. Urine output has been 0.3-0.4 mL/kg/hr over the past 12 hours. ECG shows no peaked T waves.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Furosemide infusion to increase urine output

question.explanation:
Per KDIGO 2012, RRT is indicated for AKI only when an emergent complication is present: refractory hyperkalemia, severe/refractory metabolic acidosis, volume overload unresponsive to diuretics, uremic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding), or a dialyzable toxin. This patient has AKI stage 3 (creatinine >3x baseline), but potassium 5.3 mEq/L and bicarbonate 19 mEq/L are mild and non-refractory, he is euvolemic on exam, and there are no uremic signs. None of the KDIGO emergent triggers are met.

The AKIKI (2016) and STARRT-AKI (2020) trials specifically tested accelerated/early RRT initiation versus a watchful-waiting strategy (initiating only when a strict emergent indication develops) in critically ill patients with severe AKI, including many with stage 3 disease. Both showed no mortality benefit from early RRT, and AKIKI showed harm signals (more catheter-related bloodstream infections) with earlier dialysis. The correct strategy here is close monitoring of potassium, acid-base status, volume status, and urine output, with RRT reserved for if/when an emergent indication emerges — the creatinine trajectory or oliguria alone does not mandate dialysis.

wrong_explanations.why: AKI stage 3 by creatinine criteria alone is not an indication for RRT; AKIKI and STARRT-AKI showed no benefit (and possible harm) from early RRT absent an emergent trigger, which is not present here.

Loop diuretics do not improve renal recovery, reduce RRT need, or improve mortality in AKI and are not indicated in a euvolemic patient without pulmonary edema; using them here would not treat the underlying injury.
Bicarbonate 19 mEq/L is only mildly reduced and does not meet criteria for severe/refractory acidosis requiring correction; empiric bicarbonate has no proven benefit and risks volume/sodium overload.
Renal-dose dopamine has been definitively shown (ANZICS Clinical Trials Group) to lack renoprotective effect and does not prevent progression or need for RRT in AKI; it is no longer recommended.

question.difficulty_rationale: Requires integrating AKI staging, hemodynamic/exam data, and lab values against the specific KDIGO emergent-indication checklist rather than reflexively equating high creatinine or oliguria with a need for dialysis.
reasoning_steps: Recognize KDIGO stage 3 AKI based on creatinine tripling from baseline
Identify the clinical context as cardiac surgery-associated/contrast-associated intrinsic AKI with adequate resuscitation (not prerenal)
Systematically screen for the KDIGO emergent RRT triggers: refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, volume overload, uremic emergency, dialyzable toxin
Determine that potassium 5.3 and bicarbonate 19 are mild/non-refractory and the patient is euvolemic without uremic signs, so no trigger is met
Apply AKIKI/STARRT-AKI evidence that early RRT confers no benefit absent an emergent indication, favoring watchful waiting

talk.key_point: Initiate RRT in AKI only for refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, volume overload, uremic complications, or a dialyzable toxin — the degree of creatinine rise or oliguria alone, even KDIGO stage 3, is not itself an indication.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Indications for renal replacement therapy in AKI (watchful waiting vs early RRT)

board_pearls: Cardiac surgery and recent contrast exposure are classic precipitants of intrinsic AKI (ATN) in the post-operative setting.

KDIGO 2012 defines RRT indications as AEIOU-style emergencies: refractory hyperkalemia/acidosis, volume overload, uremic complications, and dialyzable intoxications — not a specific creatinine or KDIGO stage cutoff.
The key discriminator from 'start dialysis now' is the absence of refractory/severe derangement: mild hyperkalemia and mild acidosis without ECG changes or uremic signs do not qualify as emergent.

AKIKI (2016) and STARRT-AKI (2020) are the landmark trials showing no mortality benefit — and in AKIKI's case, more catheter-related infections — with early/accelerated RRT versus watchful waiting in critically ill patients with severe AKI.

The most common trap is equating a tripled creatinine (stage 3 AKI) with an automatic dialysis indication; the guideline and trial evidence require an emergent complication, not just a lab-defined AKI stage.
teaching_points: AKI staging (KDIGO 1/2/3) determines prognosis and monitoring intensity but does not by itself dictate RRT initiation.
Loop diuretics and low-dose dopamine have no proven role in altering the natural history of AKI and should not be used to 'convert' oliguric to non-oliguric AKI.
When no emergent RRT trigger is present, the evidence-based approach is close observation with serial labs and urine output trends, initiating RRT only if/when a true indication develops.
summary_points: RRT in AKI is indicated for emergent complications, not for AKI stage or oliguria alone.
AKIKI and STARRT-AKI confirm watchful waiting is as safe as early RRT and avoids unnecessary catheter-related risk.

visual_memory_card.bottom_right: Trap: assuming high creatinine alone mandates dialysis

question.stem:
A 64-year-old man is evaluated in the ICU on hospital day 3 for oliguria. He was admitted with Escherichia coli bacteremia from pyelonephritis and septic shock requiring norepinephrine, which was discontinued 8 hours ago. He received 4 L of balanced crystalloid. Urine output has been 15 mL/h for the past 12 hours. He is receiving piperacillin-tazobactam. Home lisinopril and ibuprofen were held on admission. He is alert and denies nausea.

Temperature 37.2 C, BP 112/68 mm Hg, HR 88/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula. JVP is not elevated, lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema, asterixis, or pericardial rub.

Sodium 136 mEq/L, potassium 5.3 mEq/L, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L, BUN 62 mg/dL, creatinine 3.6 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL). Arterial pH 7.31, PaCO2 34 mm Hg. CXR shows clear lung fields. Bladder US shows no hydronephrosis; post-void residual 20 mL.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Continue supportive care with close monitoring

question.explanation:
KDIGO 2012 AKI recommends initiating renal replacement therapy (RRT) "emergently when life-threatening changes in fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance exist," and otherwise deciding on the basis of the broader clinical context and trajectory rather than a creatinine or urine-output threshold alone. This patient has KDIGO stage 3 AKI (creatinine >3x baseline) from septic/ischemic ATN compounded by ACEi and NSAID exposure, but has NO urgent indication: potassium 5.3 mEq/L (not refractory), pH 7.31 with bicarbonate 18 mEq/L (compensated, not severe), euvolemia with clear lungs, no encephalopathy, pericarditis, or dialyzable intoxication. Postrenal obstruction is excluded by US.

Two randomized trials directly address the close second choice. AKIKI (2016) and STARRT-AKI (2020) both showed that accelerated RRT in severe AKI without urgent indications conferred no mortality benefit; in STARRT-AKI, accelerated initiation increased adverse events (hypotension, catheter complications) and 90-day RRT dependence. Roughly half of patients randomized to a watchful-waiting strategy recovered without ever needing dialysis. AKIKI-2 further showed that delaying beyond a standard delayed strategy provided no additional benefit.

Thus the guideline-concordant next step is continued supportive management: sustain renal perfusion and MAP, keep nephrotoxins (lisinopril, NSAIDs) withheld, renally dose piperacillin-tazobactam, avoid contrast, treat hyperkalemia medically, and monitor potassium, acid-base status, volume, and urine output closely so RRT can be started promptly if an indication emerges.

wrong_explanations.why: Bicarbonate therapy is generally reserved for severe metabolic acidemia (pH <7.1-7.2). At pH 7.31 with appropriate respiratory compensation, alkali adds sodium and volume load, worsens intracellular acidosis and ionized hypocalcemia, and does not alter AKI trajectory or need for RRT.

This is the popular trap. AKIKI and STARRT-AKI showed accelerated RRT in stage 3 AKI without urgent indications does not improve survival and increases catheter complications, hypotension, and 90-day dialysis dependence. Stage 3 creatinine and oliguria alone are not indications.

Loop diuretics may increase urine output but do not prevent or shorten AKI, reduce RRT need, or improve mortality; KDIGO recommends against using diuretics to treat AKI. In a euvolemic patient they risk hypovolemia and worsening ischemic tubular injury.

Low-dose "renal-dose" dopamine has been repeatedly shown ineffective for preventing or treating AKI and is explicitly recommended against by KDIGO; it adds tachyarrhythmia and splanchnic ischemia risk without improving renal recovery.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must stage the AKI, systematically exclude each urgent RRT indication using specific lab and exam data, and then apply randomized-trial evidence on initiation timing to reject three physiologically tempting pharmacologic interventions.
reasoning_steps: Stage the AKI: creatinine 3.6 from baseline 1.0 with oliguria = KDIGO stage 3, from septic ATN plus ACEi/NSAID exposure.
Exclude postrenal and rapidly reversible causes: normal bladder US, no hydronephrosis, low PVR, shock already resolved with vasopressors off.
Screen for each urgent RRT indication: hyperkalemia not refractory, acidemia mild and compensated, euvolemic with clear CXR, no uremic encephalopathy/pericarditis, no dialyzable toxin.
Apply AKIKI/STARRT-AKI: accelerated RRT without urgent indication offers no mortality benefit and increases dialysis dependence and catheter complications.
Reject non-evidence-based pharmacologic options (bicarbonate, loop diuretic, renal-dose dopamine) and choose continued supportive care with close monitoring.

talk.key_point: In stage 3 AKI without refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidemia, volume overload, uremic complications, or a dialyzable toxin, continue supportive care and monitor closely rather than starting early RRT [1,3].

abim_classification.specific_topic: AKI: indications and timing of renal replacement therapy

board_pearls: Septic AKI reflects tubular injury plus microvascular and RAS-mediated efferent tone loss; withholding ACEi/NSAIDs and restoring MAP addresses the driver, whereas dialysis only substitutes for lost clearance.

KDIGO 2012 states RRT should be started emergently for life-threatening fluid, electrolyte, or acid-base derangements, and otherwise decided on the whole clinical context rather than any single BUN or creatinine threshold [1].

The discriminator between early RRT and watchful waiting is the presence of an urgent indication (refractory K, pH <7.1-7.15, refractory volume overload, uremic pericarditis/encephalopathy, dialyzable toxin), not the AKI stage or urine output [1].

STARRT-AKI (NEJM 2020, n=3019) found identical 90-day mortality with accelerated versus standard RRT initiation but MORE adverse events and greater RRT dependence at 90 days in the accelerated arm; AKIKI showed nearly half of delayed-strategy patients never required dialysis [2,3].

The classic trap is equating KDIGO stage 3 plus oliguria with a dialysis indication; premature catheter placement exposes the patient to hypotension, bleeding, infection, and loss of residual renal function without survival benefit [3].
teaching_points: Approach every AKI with the three-bucket framework (prerenal, intrinsic, postrenal): obstruction was excluded here by renal/bladder ultrasound, and the ischemic-septic ATN diagnosis is supported by the shock course plus ACEi/NSAID exposure [1].

Supportive AKI care means sustaining perfusion and MAP, stopping nephrotoxins, renally dose-adjusting antibiotics, avoiding contrast, managing potassium medically, and reassessing volume and labs at least daily [1].
Neither loop diuretics nor low-dose dopamine improves AKI outcomes; increasing urine output is not the same as improving glomerular filtration and can create false reassurance [1].
summary_points: Stage 3 AKI alone does not mandate dialysis; look for a specific urgent indication [1].
Accelerated RRT in AKI shows no mortality benefit and more harm (AKIKI, STARRT-AKI, AKIKI-2) [2,3,4].

visual_memory_card.top_left: Stage 3 AKI, K 5.3, euvolemic
visual_memory_card.top_right: Septic ATN; clearance loss without lethal derangement
visual_memory_card.bottom_left: No urgent indication means watchful waiting
visual_memory_card.bottom_right: Do not dialyze for creatinine or oliguria

gemini_errors: Stem labels a creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL in a 74-year-old as 'baseline CKD' without any supporting data (eGFR/albuminuria/chronicity); this is a normal-range creatinine and mislabels the baseline.
STARRT-AKI is cited with an incorrect PMID (32738793); the NEJM 2020 STARRT-AKI trial is PMID 32668114 — a citation-accuracy failure.
ABIM blueprint weight for nephrology listed as 7% (actual IM blueprint nephrology ≈6%) — trivial, non-clinical.
claude_errors: Internal lab inconsistency: pH 7.31 with HCO3 18 mEq/L and PaCO2 34 mm Hg is not consistent (Henderson–Hasselbalch yields pH ≈7.34–7.35); minor but a solver checking compensation will notice.

Slight overstatement of guideline strength: KDIGO 2012 'suggests' not using diuretics to TREAT AKI except for volume overload (2C, not a strong recommendation); the strong 1B recommendation applies to prevention. (The 1A recommendation against low-dose dopamine is correctly characterized.)
judge.why: Both items teach the same high-yield point correctly — KDIGO 2012 reserves emergent RRT for refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, refractory volume overload, uremic complications, or dialyzable toxins, and AKIKI/STARRT-AKI show no mortality benefit to accelerated initiation. B is superior on citation honesty (correct PMIDs, correct NEJM/Lancet volume-page data, correct blueprint weight, and appropriate addition of AKIKI-2 with a conservative 'no additional benefit' claim) and on trial-detail fidelity (STARRT-AKI's excess adverse events and 90-day RRT dependence; AKIKI's ~49% of delayed patients never dialyzed). B also gives a richer, more testable workup (postrenal excluded by ultrasound/PVR, nephrotoxin withdrawal, renal dosing of pip-tazo, ABG-based acid-base reasoning), which raises teaching value for an IM resident. A is accurate in substance and correctly attributes the renal-dose dopamine data to the ANZICS trial, but has a wrong STARRT-AKI PMID, mislabels a normal creatinine as CKD, and offers less granular trial data. B's flaws (one internally inconsistent ABG and a mild overstatement of the KDIGO diuretic recommendation grade) are less consequential.

sections.heading: Physiology: Why a Sick Liver Shuts Down the Kidney
points: It starts in the sinusoid: fibrosis, regenerative nodules and activated stellate cells raise intrahepatic resistance. Increased shear stress in the splanchnic bed then upregulates endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), and NO plus carbon monoxide, prostacyclin and endocannabinoids produce profound SPLANCHNIC ARTERIAL VASODILATION.

Vasodilation sequesters blood volume in the splanchnic circulation. Total plasma volume is HIGH but EFFECTIVE arterial blood volume is LOW — a state of arterial underfilling with a low systemic vascular resistance, low mean arterial pressure, high cardiac output profile.

Baroreceptors read the underfilling and fire three vasoconstrictor systems: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (RAAS), sympathetic nervous system, and non-osmotic ADH release. Angiotensin II and norepinephrine constrict the renal afferent arteriole; ADH drives free water retention (hence the hyponatremia that so often accompanies HRS).

Because the splanchnic bed is refractory to these vasoconstrictors (NO-mediated), the kidney absorbs the entire vasoconstrictor burden. Renal blood flow falls, GFR falls, and avid tubular sodium reabsorption produces urine sodium typically <10 mEq/L with FENa <0.2% — yet the tubules are structurally INTACT. HRS is functional, and it is reversible.

A second hit is inflammatory: portal hypertension causes gut bacterial translocation, and PAMPs/DAMPs (endotoxin) engage toll-like receptors, generating cytokines that impair renal microcirculatory autoregulation and cause direct tubular stress. This is why infection — especially SBP — is the classic precipitant, and why severe HRS blends into a tubular injury phenotype.

A third hit is cardiac: cirrhotic cardiomyopathy (blunted beta-adrenergic responsiveness, impaired contractile reserve, prolonged QT) means the heart cannot raise output enough to defend renal perfusion once vasodilation is severe. Relative cardiac insufficiency, not just vasodilation, predicts HRS.
sections.mechanism: HRS is arterial underfilling from NO-driven splanchnic vasodilation, plus systemic inflammation and blunted cardiac reserve, producing maximal renal vasoconstriction with histologically normal tubules — so any therapy that restores effective arterial volume and splanchnic tone can reverse it.
sections.teaching_pearl: HRS is the only common cause of AKI where kidneys transplanted from the affected patient work normally in a recipient — the lesion is in the circulation, not the nephron.
sections.board_tip: Bland urinalysis + urine Na <10 + FENa <0.2% + ascites + no volume response = HRS-AKI, not ATN. If you see granular casts, proteinuria >500 mg/day, or hematuria, look for intrinsic disease (IgA nephropathy in cirrhosis, HCV cryoglobulinemic MPGN, bile-cast nephropathy).

sections.heading: Diagnosis: HRS-AKI Is a Diagnosis of Non-Response, Not of Exclusion Alone
points: Terminology matters: the old 'type 1/type 2' framing was replaced by the ICA 2015 revision — HRS-AKI (formerly type 1) uses KDIGO AKI criteria, and there is no longer a fixed creatinine cutoff of 2.5 mg/dL that must be reached before diagnosis or treatment. Slow chronic decline is HRS-CKD (formerly type 2) [1,3,8].

Criteria: (1) cirrhosis with ascites; (2) AKI — Cr rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h or ≥50% from baseline within 7 days; (3) no sustained improvement after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal PLUS volume expansion with albumin 1 g/kg/day (max 100 g/day); (4) absence of shock; (5) no current or recent nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast); (6) no structural kidney injury — proteinuria <500 mg/day, <50 RBC/hpf, normal renal ultrasound [1,3].

Always hunt the precipitant in parallel: diagnostic paracentesis in EVERY cirrhotic with AKI (ascitic PMN ≥250/mm3 = SBP), plus cultures, GI bleed evaluation, over-diuresis, large-volume paracentesis without albumin, lactulose-related hypovolemic diarrhea, and NSAID/ACEi/ARB exposure [1].

Differential by mechanism: hypovolemic prerenal AKI (responds to volume — that is the point of the 2-day albumin challenge), ATN from prolonged shock or sepsis, bile-cast nephropathy in severe hyperbilirubinemia, abdominal compartment physiology from tense ascites, and post-renal obstruction. Creatinine systematically OVERESTIMATES GFR in cirrhosis — sarcopenia lowers creatinine generation and bilirubin interferes with the Jaffe assay — so a Cr of 1.2 mg/dL may represent a GFR of 40 [1].

Biomarkers: urinary NGAL is the best-studied discriminator, markedly elevated in ATN, intermediate in HRS, and low in prerenal azotemia. It is not universally available and is not required by AASLD 2021 for diagnosis [1].
sections.teaching_pearl: Do not wait for the creatinine to be dramatic. Under ICA/AASLD criteria, HRS-AKI can be diagnosed and treated at stage 1 AKI, and every day of delay lowers the reversal rate and raises the post-treatment creatinine plateau.
sections.board_tip: The 2-day albumin/diuretic-withdrawal challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic — a stem where the creatinine falls with volume is prerenal AKI, not HRS.

sections.heading: Treatment: Refill the Arterial Circulation, Then Get to Transplant
points: FIRST-LINE per AASLD 2021: TERLIPRESSIN plus ALBUMIN. Terlipressin was FDA-approved in September 2022 (after the guidance was written but consistent with it), given as 1 mg IV q6h (or continuous infusion 2 mg/day) escalating to 2 mg q6h if creatinine has not fallen ≥25% by day 3, with albumin 20-40 g/day [1,2].

CONFIRM (NEJM 2021) is the pivotal trial: verified HRS reversal 32% with terlipressin+albumin vs 17% with placebo+albumin (p=0.006). But it also defined the toxicity — respiratory failure occurred in 10% vs 3%, and 90-day mortality was numerically worse in that subgroup. Do NOT start terlipressin in patients with hypoxia, volume overload, or ACLF grade 3, and cap albumin (roughly ≤100 g/day) because most respiratory events were fluid-driven [2].

Supportive moves that are non-negotiable: STOP diuretics, stop beta blockers if MAP is low or ascites is refractory, stop NSAIDs/ACEi/ARB/aminoglycosides, avoid contrast, and treat any infection immediately with broad-spectrum antibiotics. In SBP, give albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 — this reduces HRS from 33% to 10% and mortality from 29% to 10% [1,4].

ALTERNATIVES when terlipressin is unavailable or contraindicated: norepinephrine titrated to raise MAP by 10 mmHg in an ICU setting (comparable efficacy in small RCTs and preferred by many US intensivists), or midodrine + octreotide + albumin — the weakest option, shown inferior to terlipressin (reversal 70% vs 29% in Cavallin et al.) and used only when nothing else is available [1,5].

TIPS can improve renal function by decompressing the portal system and reducing the vasodilatory/RAAS stimulus, but it is NOT first-line for HRS-AKI; it is limited by hepatic encephalopathy and bilirubin/MELD thresholds and lacks RCT support in HRS [1,7].

Renal replacement therapy is a BRIDGE, not a treatment — indicated for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, or uremic complications per standard KDIGO AKI indications, and justified mainly in transplant candidates or those with a reversible precipitant [1,8].

LIVER TRANSPLANT is definitive because it removes the driver. Prolonged pre-transplant dialysis (generally >4-6 weeks) or established CKD triggers consideration of simultaneous liver-kidney transplant. Prevention is the highest-yield intervention: albumin 6-8 g per liter removed for paracentesis >5 L, SBP prophylaxis after an episode, and long-term albumin in select decompensated patients (ANSWER trial showed survival benefit; not a strong AASLD recommendation) [1,6].
sections.mechanism: Terlipressin is a V1 receptor agonist prodrug of lysine-vasopressin: it constricts splanchnic arterioles, translocating pooled blood back into the effective arterial compartment. Rising effective arterial volume shuts off RAAS, sympathetic and ADH drive, which releases the renal afferent arteriole from vasoconstriction and restores GFR. Albumin adds oncotic volume expansion plus non-oncotic effects — endotoxin and reactive-oxygen scavenging and stabilization of endothelial function. Norepinephrine achieves the same hemodynamic endpoint via alpha-1 receptors; midodrine (oral alpha-1 agonist) plus octreotide (inhibits splanchnic vasodilator peptides) is a pharmacologically weaker imitation.
sections.teaching_pearl: The therapeutic target is a MAP rise of about 10 mmHg — if MAP does not budge, you have not corrected the physiology and creatinine will not fall regardless of which vasoconstrictor you chose.
sections.board_tip: Two albumin doses residents must memorize: SBP — 1.5 g/kg day 1 and 1.0 g/kg day 3; large-volume paracentesis >5 L — 6-8 g per liter removed. Both prevent HRS [1,4].

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: Untreated HRS-AKI is one of the most lethal complications of cirrhosis: median survival historically measured in weeks, with in-hospital mortality commonly 40-60% and near-uniform death by 3 months without reversal or transplant [1].
Even with best therapy, only about a third of patients achieve verified HRS reversal, and roughly one in five who respond will relapse after treatment stops — retreatment is reasonable [2].

Prognosis is driven by (1) baseline creatinine at treatment initiation — lower is better, which is the argument for early treatment; (2) the MAP response in the first 3 days; (3) bilirubin/MELD; and (4) ACLF grade and number of failing organs. Absence of any creatinine decline by day 4 predicts non-response [1,2].

HRS reversal improves survival mainly by buying transplant eligibility and time; it does not change the underlying liver disease. Post-liver-transplant survival remains good, but pre-transplant HRS/dialysis predicts post-transplant CKD.
Because HRS is a marker of end-stage portal hypertensive physiology, every episode should trigger transplant evaluation AND a parallel goals-of-care conversation for patients who are not candidates.
sections.teaching_pearl: HRS is not a kidney disease with a liver problem — it is end-stage liver disease presenting through the kidney. The prognosis tracks the liver, not the creatinine.
sections.board_tip: A cirrhotic with an episode of HRS-AKI who is not a transplant candidate has a prognosis comparable to many metastatic cancers — palliative care referral is guideline-concordant care, not giving up.

summary_points: MECHANISM: NO-driven splanchnic arterial vasodilation from portal hypertension creates effective arterial hypovolemia; compensatory RAAS/sympathetic/ADH activation vasoconstricts the kidney while tubules remain structurally normal — HRS is functional and reversible.

DIAGNOSIS: HRS-AKI = cirrhosis with ascites + KDIGO AKI + NO response to 2 days off diuretics with albumin 1 g/kg/day + no shock, no nephrotoxins, no structural disease (proteinuria <500 mg/day, <50 RBC/hpf, normal renal US). The old creatinine >2.5 mg/dL threshold is obsolete [1,3].

TREATMENT: terlipressin + albumin is first-line per AASLD 2021 and FDA-approved since Sept 2022; CONFIRM showed 32% vs 17% HRS reversal but 10% respiratory failure — avoid in hypoxia, volume overload, or ACLF-3. Norepinephrine in the ICU is the practical alternative; midodrine/octreotide is the weakest option [1,2,5].
PREVENTION beats rescue: albumin 1.5 g/kg then 1 g/kg for SBP cut renal impairment from 33% to 10% and mortality from 29% to 10%; albumin 6-8 g/L for paracentesis >5 L [1,4].

BIGGEST PITFALL: anchoring on a 'normal' creatinine. Sarcopenia and bilirubin assay interference make creatinine overestimate GFR in cirrhosis — treat at AKI stage 1, and always tap the abdomen looking for SBP as the precipitant [1].

Liver transplant is the only definitive therapy; prolonged dialysis pre-transplant raises the question of simultaneous liver-kidney. Every HRS episode should trigger transplant evaluation and, if ineligible, palliative care.

guideline_sources: AASLD Ascites, SBP and Hepatorenal Syndrome 2021 Practice Guidance

references.source: Biggins SW, et al. Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Management of Ascites, Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis and Hepatorenal Syndrome: 2021 Practice Guidance by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases
Wong F, et al. Terlipressin plus Albumin for the Treatment of Type 1 Hepatorenal Syndrome (CONFIRM trial)

question.stem:
A 58-year-old woman with alcohol-associated cirrhosis is hospitalized for worsening ascites. Diuretics were held on admission and she received albumin 1 g/kg/day (max 100 g/day) for 2 days for a rising creatinine, without improvement. Urine output remains under 400 mL/day. She has no fever, diarrhea, or NSAID use.

Temperature 36.9°C, BP 98/60 mmHg, HR 88/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Distended abdomen with shifting dullness; no rash, no signs of shock.

Creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL), BUN 42 mg/dL, sodium 128 mEq/L. Urinalysis: bland sediment, no proteinuria or hematuria. Urine sodium <10 mEq/L. Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys, no hydronephrosis.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation: This patient meets ICA criteria for HRS-AKI: creatinine rise despite 48 hours of diuretic withdrawal and albumin challenge, bland urinalysis, no shock, no nephrotoxins, and normal renal imaging excluding structural disease. Per the AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance, once other causes of AKI are excluded and the volume-expansion trial has failed, terlipressin plus albumin is first-line therapy for HRS-AKI (terlipressin FDA-approved 2022, supported by the CONFIRM trial showing improved HRS reversal versus placebo plus albumin) [1,2]. Terlipressin is a splanchnic vasoconstrictor that raises effective arterial blood volume, improving renal perfusion, while albumin provides oncotic support and improves circulatory function. Midodrine-octreotide-albumin is reserved as the alternative regimen only when terlipressin is unavailable or contraindicated, and is less effective at reversing HRS. Continuing albumin alone has already failed as a diagnostic/therapeutic trial. TIPS and hemodialysis are not indicated as initial therapy for HRS-AKI; TIPS is used for refractory ascites/variceal bleeding, and dialysis is reserved for refractory cases as a bridge to transplant, which remains the only definitive cure.

wrong_explanations.why: Hemodialysis is reserved for refractory HRS-AKI unresponsive to vasoconstrictor therapy or as a bridge to transplant, not initial management.
The albumin-alone challenge already failed to improve creatinine over 2 days, confirming HRS-AKI rather than prerenal azotemia; continuing it alone is inadequate.
Midodrine, octreotide, and albumin is the alternative regimen used only when terlipressin is unavailable or contraindicated; it is less effective and not first-line when terlipressin can be given.
TIPS is used for refractory ascites or variceal bleeding prophylaxis, not as acute pharmacologic therapy for HRS-AKI.

question.difficulty_rationale: Requires integrating exclusion criteria for HRS-AKI (bland sediment, low urine sodium, normal imaging, failed albumin challenge) with the specific guideline-preferred vasoconstrictor regimen over a very close alternative regimen.
reasoning_steps: Recognize AKI in a cirrhotic patient with ascites and exclude prerenal azotemia/ATN using bland urinalysis, low urine sodium, and normal renal imaging
Confirm ICA/HRS-AKI diagnostic criteria are met given creatinine rise despite diuretic withdrawal and a failed 2-day albumin challenge
Apply the AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance recommendation that terlipressin plus albumin is first-line therapy for confirmed HRS-AKI
Eliminate midodrine-octreotide-albumin as it is only the alternative when terlipressin is unavailable
Eliminate TIPS and hemodialysis as they are not indicated for initial HRS-AKI pharmacotherapy

talk.key_point: In HRS-AKI diagnosed after exclusion of other causes and a failed albumin challenge, terlipressin plus albumin is first-line therapy; midodrine-octreotide-albumin is reserved for when terlipressin is unavailable.
board_pearls: Terlipressin is a splanchnic vasopressin analog that increases effective arterial blood volume and renal perfusion pressure, the core pathophysiologic defect in HRS-AKI.
AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance and the FDA (2022, based on CONFIRM) endorse terlipressin plus albumin as first-line therapy for HRS-AKI [1,2].
The key discriminator from midodrine-octreotide-albumin is availability: the latter is reserved specifically for when terlipressin cannot be used.
The CONFIRM trial demonstrated superior HRS reversal with terlipressin plus albumin versus placebo plus albumin, though watch for pulmonary edema/respiratory failure risk with terlipressin [2].
The most common trap is choosing continued albumin alone or TIPS — albumin alone has already failed as a diagnostic trial, and TIPS/hemodialysis are not first-line acute therapies for HRS-AKI.
teaching_points: HRS-AKI diagnosis requires exclusion of shock, nephrotoxins, and structural kidney disease plus failure to improve after diuretic withdrawal and albumin challenge.
Terlipressin plus albumin is the guideline-preferred first-line pharmacologic therapy for HRS-AKI, per AASLD 2021 and FDA approval in 2022.
Liver transplantation remains the only definitive cure for HRS-AKI; pharmacotherapy and dialysis are bridges, not cures.
summary_points: Terlipressin plus albumin is first-line for confirmed HRS-AKI after excluding other AKI causes and failing a volume-expansion trial.

visual_memory_card.top_left: Bland sediment, low urine Na, failed albumin trial
visual_memory_card.top_right: Terlipressin vasoconstricts splanchnic bed, improves renal perfusion
visual_memory_card.bottom_left: Terlipressin + albumin = first-line HRS-AKI therapy
visual_memory_card.bottom_right: Don't pick midodrine-octreotide-albumin when terlipressin is available

question.stem:
A 58-year-old man is evaluated in the hospital for rising creatinine. He has alcohol-related cirrhosis with ascites; his diuretic doses were increased 2 weeks ago for worsening abdominal distention. Baseline creatinine was 0.8 mg/dL. Over 5 days it rose to 2.4 mg/dL, with declining urine output. Diuretics were stopped 48 hours ago and albumin 1 g/kg daily was given for 2 days without improvement. He takes no NSAIDs and has had no contrast exposure or gastrointestinal bleeding.

Temperature 36.9 C, BP 96/58 mm Hg, HR 88/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air. He has tense ascites and 1+ ankle edema. No asterixis or encephalopathy.

Sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, total bilirubin 4.1 mg/dL, INR 1.8, lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Urinalysis: no protein, no blood, no casts; urine sodium 8 mEq/L. Renal US shows normal kidneys without hydronephrosis. Diagnostic paracentesis: 90 PMNs/mm3.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Begin norepinephrine and albumin in the ICU

question.explanation:
This patient meets ICA criteria for HRS-AKI: cirrhosis with ascites, stage 2 AKI, no improvement after 48 hours of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin volume expansion, bland urinalysis with urine sodium <10 mEq/L, no shock, no nephrotoxin exposure, and no structural or obstructive disease on ultrasound. Ascitic PMN count <250/mm3 excludes SBP as an untreated precipitant. The physiology is splanchnic arterial vasodilation with effective arterial underfilling and intense renal vasoconstriction — hence the treatment is systemic vasoconstriction, not more volume or diuresis.

The AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance states that for HRS-AKI, terlipressin plus albumin is first-line pharmacotherapy, with midodrine/octreotide plus albumin reserved for settings where terlipressin is unavailable [1]. Terlipressin was FDA-approved in September 2022 on the basis of CONFIRM, which showed significantly higher rates of HRS reversal versus placebo (29% vs 16%) [2]. Terlipressin should be avoided when serum creatinine exceeds ~5 mg/dL, in ACLF grade 3, or with baseline hypoxemia because of respiratory failure risk; this patient has none of these and is a candidate. Simultaneously, he should be referred for liver transplantation evaluation, which remains the definitive therapy [1].

Because creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL, oxygenation is normal, and there is no grade 3 ACLF, terlipressin with concomitant albumin is unambiguously the preferred initial vasoconstrictor here [1,2].

wrong_explanations.why: Midodrine plus octreotide with albumin is the least effective vasoconstrictor regimen and is explicitly a fallback for when terlipressin is unavailable in the AASLD 2021 guidance — not first-line in a patient who is a terlipressin candidate.

Norepinephrine plus albumin is an acceptable alternative, but it requires ICU-level care and central access; in a hemodynamically stable ward patient without shock (lactate 1.4 mmol/L), terlipressin is the guideline-preferred first-line agent.

Paracentesis relieves symptomatic tense ascites but does not reverse HRS physiology; large-volume removal without adequate albumin can worsen circulatory dysfunction and AKI. It does not substitute for vasoconstrictor therapy.

Resuming diuretics is harmful: diuretic withdrawal is part of the diagnostic and therapeutic pathway for HRS-AKI. Further natriuresis would worsen effective arterial underfilling and renal hypoperfusion.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must confirm HRS-AKI by sequentially excluding hypovolemia, SBP, ATN, and obstruction, then choose among four genuinely used vasoconstrictor or ascites-directed strategies ranked by guideline preference.
reasoning_steps: Recognize stage 2 AKI in cirrhosis with ascites and characterize it using urine findings (bland sediment, urine sodium 8 mEq/L) as functional rather than intrinsic.
Note that 48 hours of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin expansion failed, excluding simple hypovolemic prerenal AKI and satisfying ICA criteria for HRS-AKI.
Exclude competing precipitants: ascitic PMN 90/mm3 rules out SBP, normal lactate/BP rules out septic shock, no NSAIDs or contrast, normal renal US rules out obstruction.
Apply the pathophysiology — splanchnic vasodilation with renal vasoconstriction — to select systemic vasoconstriction plus albumin rather than more diuresis or paracentesis.

Rank vasoconstrictor options per AASLD 2021: terlipressin plus albumin first-line; verify no contraindication (creatinine <5 mg/dL, no hypoxemia, no ACLF grade 3) before choosing it over norepinephrine or midodrine/octreotide.

talk.key_point: In HRS-AKI that persists after diuretic withdrawal and albumin expansion, terlipressin plus albumin is first-line; avoid terlipressin with creatinine >5 mg/dL, hypoxemia, or ACLF grade 3. [1]

abim_classification.specific_topic: Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI): diagnosis and terlipressin therapy

board_pearls: HRS-AKI is functional renal failure from splanchnic vasodilation and effective arterial underfilling; vasoconstrictors plus albumin restore renal perfusion pressure, which is why volume alone fails. [1]
AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance: terlipressin plus albumin is first-line for HRS-AKI; midodrine/octreotide plus albumin only if terlipressin is unavailable; transplant is definitive. [1]

The discriminator against midodrine/octreotide is drug availability, not patient factors — if terlipressin can be given and no contraindication exists, the oral/subcutaneous regimen is inferior therapy. [1]
CONFIRM (NEJM 2021) drove FDA approval of terlipressin in September 2022: HRS reversal 29% vs 16% with placebo, offset by more respiratory failure — hence exclusion of hypoxemic patients. [2]
The classic trap is resuming or escalating diuretics for the ascites and edema; diuretic withdrawal is required both to diagnose HRS-AKI and to avoid worsening renal hypoperfusion. [1]
teaching_points: ICA HRS-AKI criteria: cirrhosis with ascites, AKI by KDIGO, no response to 2 days of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin 1 g/kg/day, absence of shock, no nephrotoxins, and no proteinuria/hematuria/structural disease. [1,3]
Always exclude SBP with diagnostic paracentesis in any cirrhotic patient with AKI: PMN ≥250/mm3 mandates cefotaxime plus albumin (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3), which itself prevents HRS. [1]
Every patient started on vasoconstrictor therapy for HRS-AKI should be simultaneously evaluated for liver transplantation; pharmacotherapy is a bridge, not a cure. [1]
summary_points: Cirrhosis + AKI unresponsive to diuretic withdrawal and albumin, with bland urine and urine sodium <10 mEq/L, equals HRS-AKI — treat with terlipressin plus albumin and refer for transplant. [1,2]

visual_memory_card.bottom_left: Terlipressin + albumin is first-line HRS-AKI
visual_memory_card.bottom_right: Do not restart diuretics or give octreotide first

gemini_errors: No diagnostic paracentesis is performed or mentioned in a cirrhotic patient with worsening ascites and AKI; SBP is not excluded before labeling HRS-AKI, which is a required step in the AASLD/ICA pathway (an omission that makes the stated diagnostic certainty overstated).
Blueprint weight listed as 10% for GI/Hepatology (ABIM IM blueprint is 9%) — non-clinical but inaccurate.
claude_errors: Minor: CONFIRM reversal figures quoted as 29% vs 16% — these are the FDA-label 'verified HRS reversal' numbers; the NEJM publication reported 32% vs 17% for verified reversal, so attributing 29%/16% directly to the NEJM trial is imprecise.

Minor: urine sodium <10 mEq/L is presented as part of the ICA HRS-AKI criteria in the explanation; low urine sodium is supportive but not a formal ICA criterion (the teaching points list it correctly).
judge.why: Both correctly identify HRS-AKI and correctly rank terlipressin+albumin as first-line per AASLD 2021 with midodrine/octreotide/albumin as the fallback when terlipressin is unavailable, and both correctly attribute FDA approval (2022) to CONFIRM. A is superior on teaching value and guideline fidelity: it includes the mandatory diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP (PMN 90/mm3), stages the AKI, offers norepinephrine as a genuine guideline-endorsed alternative (a far better discriminator than B's obviously wrong TIPS/dialysis options), specifies terlipressin safety exclusions (SCr ≥5 mg/dL, ACLF grade 3, hypoxemia), and adds the SBP albumin dosing and transplant-referral pearls. B is accurate but thinner, omits SBP exclusion and norepinephrine, and omits terlipressin contraindications; its distractors make the vignette easier than board level. A's only issues are small numeric/criteria imprecisions; neither artifact overstates recommendation strength or misattributes claims to sources.
