talk.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
talk.subtitle: From alveolar defense breakdown to the 2025 ATS-IDSA split on steroids and duration
guideline_sources: ATS 2025 CAP Update (IDSA did not endorse in full)
IDSA/ATS 2019 CAP Guideline (site-of-care and empiric regimens still standard)

references.source: ATS 2025 Guideline Update: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (IDSA endorsed 8/10 recommendations, rejected 2 on antibiotics in viral-positive patients)
IDSA/ATS Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with CAP
CAPE-COD Trial: Hydrocortisone in Severe Community-Acquired Pneumonia (NEJM)

sections.heading: Physiology → Pathophysiology: How the Lung Loses the Fight
points: Normal lower respiratory defense = mucociliary escalator (ciliated epithelium + mucus layer trapping particles), cough reflex, and alveolar macrophages performing phagocytosis/killing before organisms reach the alveolar space.

CAP happens when an inoculum overwhelms these defenses (aspiration of oropharyngeal flora, viral epithelial injury exposing receptors, or an unusually virulent/high-burden organism like Streptococcus pneumoniae).

Once organisms reach alveoli, macrophages release IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha → recruits neutrophils → capillary leak floods alveoli with protein-rich exudate, red cells, and fibrin (the classic lobar consolidation on imaging and on gross pathology).

Filled alveoli cannot participate in gas exchange but are still perfused → intrapulmonary shunt physiology → hypoxemia that does NOT correct easily with supplemental O2 in severe cases (true shunt vs V/Q mismatch).

Systemic spillover of the same cytokines drives fever, tachypnea (chemoreceptor + mechanoreceptor stimulation), tachycardia, and in severe disease, the SIRS/sepsis phenotype with hypotension from vasodilation and capillary leak.
sections.mechanism: The clinical picture of CAP is a direct readout of the innate immune response — the exudative alveolar filling produces the infiltrate and hypoxemia, and the cytokine cascade produces the fever/tachypnea/hemodynamic findings; this is also exactly why an overzealous inflammatory response (not just bug burden) can independently drive severity, which is the physiologic rationale behind steroids in severe CAP discussed below.
sections.teaching_pearl: Lobar consolidation with a rapid clinical course points toward a bacterial (often pneumococcal) etiology because the alveolar exudative response is intense and localized; patchy, multifocal, slower-onset disease raises atypical/viral etiologies.
sections.board_tip: Hypoxemia in pneumonia is largely shunt physiology (perfused but non-ventilated alveoli) — this is why severe CAP hypoxemia can be refractory to FiO2 titration alone and may need PEEP/positioning strategies.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Site-of-Care Decision
points: CXR confirms the infiltrate — required to make the diagnosis distinct from bronchitis; findings lag symptoms by 24-48h and can be falsely negative in dehydration or neutropenia.

CURB-65 (confusion, BUN >19, RR ≥30, BP <90/60, age ≥65) or Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) formally risk-stratify site of care — this operationalizes the physiology above: more criteria met = more systemic cytokine spillover = higher mortality risk.

Blood cultures, sputum Gram stain/culture, and urinary Legionella/pneumococcal antigens are reserved for severe CAP or those with specific risk factors (recent hospitalization, prior MRSA/Pseudomonas isolation) — not routine in low-risk outpatients, since yield is low and rarely changes empiric therapy.

ATS minor criteria (RR ≥30, PaO2/FiO2 ≤250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, uremia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension needing aggressive fluids) — meeting ≥3 defines severe CAP and should trigger ICU-level evaluation.

MRSA and Pseudomonas risk is now individualized (prior isolation of these organisms from respiratory tract, especially within the last year) rather than using the retired 'HCAP' category — a change carried forward unchanged from 2019 into ATS 2025[1,2].
sections.teaching_pearl: Do not order sputum cultures or blood cultures reflexively on every outpatient CAP — reserve microbiologic workup for severe disease or specific risk factors; this mirrors general antimicrobial stewardship logic across ID.
sections.board_tip: CURB-65 score of 0-1 = outpatient; 2 = consider short inpatient stay or close outpatient follow-up; ≥3 = inpatient, consider ICU if ATS minor criteria met.

sections.heading: Treatment: The Contested 2025 Update
points: Outpatient, no comorbidities: amoxicillin or doxycycline; macrolide monotherapy only where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is low[2].

Outpatient with comorbidities, or non-severe inpatient: beta-lactam (amoxicillin-clavulanate or a cephalosporin) PLUS a macrolide, or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy (levofloxacin) — unchanged from 2019[1,2].
Severe/ICU CAP: beta-lactam plus macrolide (preferred over fluoroquinolone in this tier) plus MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage if risk factors present.

HIGHEST-YIELD 2025 CHANGE: ATS 2025 now suggests CORTICOSTEROIDS in SEVERE CAP (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence), a reversal of the 2019 recommendation AGAINST routine steroids — EXCLUDING influenza pneumonia, where steroids are not recommended[1].

SHORTER DURATION: ATS 2025 conditionally recommends 3-5 days for outpatients with comorbidities and for inpatients with non-severe CAP once clinical stability is reached (minimum 3 days), down from the prior floor of ≥5 days[1].

IDSA DID NOT FULLY ENDORSE the 2025 update — it accepted 8 of 10 recommendations but explicitly rejected the two addressing antibiotic decisions in patients with a positive viral respiratory assay, arguing the evidence doesn't yet support withholding/narrowing antibiotics on viral testing alone[1]. Teach this as an unresolved, genuine society disagreement, not a settled answer.
sections.mechanism: Corticosteroids blunt the same cytokine cascade (IL-6, TNF-alpha) that drives capillary leak and alveolar flooding described above — in severe CAP, where hyperinflammation itself (not just ongoing bacterial replication) contributes to organ dysfunction, damping that response can reduce progression to respiratory failure/shock, which is the physiologic rationale behind the CAPE-COD trial finding reduced mortality with hydrocortisone in severe CAP[3]. Macrolides added to a beta-lactam serve two purposes mechanistically: atypical pathogen coverage (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila lack cell walls, so beta-lactams don't touch them) and an independent immunomodulatory/anti-inflammatory effect on neutrophil function that may itself improve outcomes.
sections.teaching_pearl: The steroid recommendation is CONDITIONAL and LOW-CERTAINTY — do not present it with the same confidence as, say, lung-protective ventilation in ARDS. Reserve it for severe CAP per the ATS 2025 definition and always exclude influenza.
sections.board_tip: Test-question trap: a patient with severe CAP AND a positive influenza PCR should still get antibiotics (bacterial coinfection is common and the ATS 2025 recommendation to narrow/withhold antibiotics based on viral testing is exactly what IDSA rejected[1]) — do not stop antibacterial coverage on a positive flu swab alone.

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: Mortality tracks directly with severity score: CURB-65 0-1 carries mortality well under 5%, while CURB-65 ≥4 approaches 30-40% — a direct clinical readout of the degree of cytokine-driven organ dysfunction.

ICU-admitted severe CAP mortality remains substantial (historically 20-50% depending on cohort and comorbidities) despite modern critical care, underscoring why early recognition via ATS minor criteria matters.
Drivers of worse prognosis: advanced age, multilobar involvement, bacteremia, immunosuppression, and delayed time-to-first-antibiotic-dose.

The CAPE-COD trial showed a 28-day mortality benefit with hydrocortisone in severe CAP (excluding influenza), providing the trial-level evidence underpinning the new ATS 2025 conditional steroid recommendation[3,1].
sections.teaching_pearl: Site-of-care decisions are not just triage logistics — CURB-65/PSI misclassification (undertriaging a severe patient to outpatient management) is one of the most preventable contributors to bad outcomes in CAP.

summary_points: CAP pathophysiology = alveolar exudative filling (shunt physiology → hypoxemia) plus systemic cytokine spillover (fever, tachypnea, hemodynamic instability) — severity findings are a direct readout of this cascade.

Site-of-care (CURB-65/PSI, ATS minor criteria) determines both antibiotic regimen and monitoring intensity; microbiologic workup should be reserved for severe or risk-factor-positive patients, not ordered reflexively.

ATS 2025 introduced two major, genuinely contested changes: corticosteroids conditionally suggested for severe CAP (except influenza) — a reversal of 2019 — and shorter treatment duration (3-5 days) for stable non-severe patients[1].
IDSA declined to endorse the ATS 2025 recommendations tying antibiotic decisions to positive viral assays — this is an active, unresolved society disagreement, not settled practice[1].

Empiric regimens are otherwise unchanged from 2019: outpatient amoxicillin/doxycycline, inpatient beta-lactam plus macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone, with individualized (not category-based) MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage[1,2].
Common pitfall: presenting the 2025 steroid recommendation with high confidence — it is conditional and low-certainty evidence, and must be framed that way on rounds and on boards.

      "minutes": "3 min",
      "points": [
        "Normal alveolus is a 0.5-micron gas-exchange membrane kept dry by tight type I epithelium and active Na+ reabsorption through type II cell ENaC/Na-K-ATPase — this is the surface that pneumonia destroys.",
        "Aspirated Streptococcus pneumoniae reaches the alveolus; its polysaccharide capsule blocks complement C3b deposition and phagocytosis, while pneumolysin (a cholesterol-dependent pore-forming toxin) lyses epithelium and cilia. Bacterial load outruns the resident alveolar macrophage.",
        "Lipoteichoic acid and peptidoglycan ligate TLR2, LPS of gram-negatives ligates TLR4 → MyD88 → NF-kB translocation → IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8. IL-8 recruits neutrophils; IL-6 drives hepatic CRP and fever via prostaglandin E2 at the hypothalamus.",
        "Neutrophil elastase, reactive oxygen species and cytokine-mediated loss of endothelial VE-cadherin junctions cause protein-rich alveolar flooding, and inflammatory exudate inactivates surfactant → alveolar collapse and reduced compliance (the 'consolidation' you percuss and hear as bronchial breath sounds and E-to-A change).",
        "Flooded but still perfused alveoli create true intrapulmonary SHUNT — this is why hypoxemia in dense lobar pneumonia responds poorly to supplemental O2 and why the A-a gradient is widened. Local inflammatory mediators (NO, prostacyclin) blunt hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening the shunt fraction.",
        "Early ABG classically shows hypoxemia with respiratory ALKALOSIS: J-receptor stimulation and cytokines drive tachypnea before CO2 retention. A normal or rising PaCO2 in a tachypneic pneumonia patient signals fatigue — an intubation warning, not reassurance.",
        "When the cytokine response becomes systemic and dysregulated, you get sepsis physiology: nitric oxide/prostacyclin-mediated vasodilation, capillary leak, and mitochondrial dysfunction → lactate elevation and organ failure. CAP is the single most common cause of sepsis. [9]"
      ],
      "mechanism": "Everything downstream — hypoxemia refractory to O2, the neutrophilic exudate, the fever and CRP, and septic shock — is one pathway: pathogen recognition receptors → NF-kB → cytokine-driven neutrophil influx and endothelial/epithelial barrier failure. Antibiotics remove the trigger; corticosteroids blunt the NF-kB-driven amplification; oxygen and PEEP recruit the flooded units.",
      "teaching_pearl": "Bacteremic pneumococcal pneumonia with a widened A-a gradient and refractory hypoxemia is shunt, not V/Q mismatch — putting the patient on 100% FiO2 with minimal PaO2 response is a physiologic diagnosis, not equipment failure.",
      "board_tip": "Sputum Gram stain with lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci plus neutrophils = pneumococcus. Elderly patient with hyponatremia, diarrhea, transaminitis and a low-grade relative bradycardia = Legionella — get the urinary antigen."
    },

      "heading": "Diagnosis and site-of-care: the two decisions that change everything",
      "minutes": "2-3 min",
      "points": [
        "Definition is clinical + radiographic: compatible symptoms (cough, fever, dyspnea, pleuritic pain) PLUS a new infiltrate. IDSA/ATS 2019 does not accept a purely clinical diagnosis. [2]",

        "Site of care is the highest-impact decision (it drives cost and mortality). Use a validated score plus clinical judgment: the 2019 guideline PREFERS the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) over CURB-65 because PSI was validated to identify low-risk outpatients. [2,7,8]",
        "Severe CAP = 1 major criterion (mechanical ventilation or vasopressors) OR >=3 minor criteria (RR >=30, PaO2/FiO2 <=250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, uremia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension requiring aggressive fluids). This label determines microbiology testing, steroid consideration, and duration. [2]",
        "Microbiologic testing is TARGETED, not reflexive: sputum culture and blood cultures for severe CAP, for patients being empirically treated for MRSA or Pseudomonas, or for those with prior isolation of those organisms. Add Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigen in severe CAP. [2]",
        "HCAP is dead — the 2019 guideline eliminated the category. Do not broaden coverage because someone came from a nursing home; assess INDIVIDUAL risk factors for MRSA and Pseudomonas (prior respiratory isolation, recent IV antibiotics, structural lung disease, hospitalization with parenteral antibiotics in 90 days). [2]",

        "In hypotension or lactate >=4, this is septic shock physiology: lactate, cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, norepinephrine first-line for fluid-refractory hypotension. [9]"
      ],
      "teaching_pearl": "If the patient does not look like the score, believe your eyes. PSI weights age heavily and will under-call a hypoxemic 40-year-old; CURB-65 has no oxygenation variable at all.",
      "board_tip": "A patient sick enough for pressors or a ventilator is severe CAP by definition — no minor criteria counting needed. That single fact unlocks the steroid and microbiology questions."
    },

      "heading": "Empiric antibiotics: pick the pathogen, not the setting",
      "minutes": "2-3 min",
      "points": [
        "Outpatient, no comorbidities (IDSA/ATS 2019, unchanged by ATS 2025): amoxicillin 1 g TID or doxycycline. A macrolide (azithromycin) is first-line ONLY where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25%. [1,2]",

[2]",

        "Influenza-positive CAP still gets antibacterials plus oseltamivir — bacterial co-infection (pneumococcus, S. aureus) is what kills. This is precisely where the 2025 society split lives: ATS made recommendations about withholding/stopping antibiotics in patients with positive viral assays, and IDSA declined to endorse those 2 recommendations while accepting the other 8. Teach the disagreement, not a false consensus. [1]"

That is why the answer is a beta-lactam PLUS an atypical agent, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV inhibition) that covers both compartments in one drug.",

      "board_tip": "Vancomycin does NOT belong in routine CAP orders. The board stem that earns MRSA coverage says 'prior respiratory culture with MRSA', 'post-influenza cavitary pneumonia', or 'recent IV antibiotics plus severe illness'."

      "minutes": "2 min",
      "points": [

        "The exception is explicit: do NOT give corticosteroids for influenza pneumonia (signal of harm — impaired viral clearance and increased mortality in observational data). [1]",
        "Evidence base: CAPE COD randomized hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (tapered, 8-14 days) in severe CAP and showed lower 28-day mortality (6.2% vs 11.9%); Torres 2015 showed reduced treatment failure in severe CAP with high inflammatory response (CRP >150). Earlier ESCAPe was neutral, which is why the recommendation is conditional. [3,4]",
        "SECOND CHANGE — DURATION: 3 to 5 days is now conditionally recommended for outpatients with comorbidities and for inpatients with non-severe CAP who reach clinical stability, with a MINIMUM of 3 days. This is shorter than the 2019 'at least 5 days'. [1,2]",
        "Clinical stability must be documented before stopping: afebrile, HR <100, RR <24, SBP >=90, SpO2 >=90% on room air, able to take oral intake, normal mentation. If not stable at day 3, do not stop. [1]",
        "Trial support for short courses: Uranga 2016 (5 days guided by stability, non-inferior) and the PTC trial (Dinh 2021 — 3 days of beta-lactam non-inferior to 8 in hospitalized non-severe CAP who were stable at day 3). [5,6]",

That is exactly the amplification loop driving hypoxemia and shock in severe CAP. In influenza, the same immunosuppression blunts antiviral T-cell responses and prolongs viral replication, which is why the drug that helps in bacterial severe CAP hurts here.",
      "teaching_pearl": "The stability criteria are the real teaching point: short-course therapy is safe because it is CONDITIONAL on the patient having responded. 'Three days' is not a blanket rule — it is 'three days plus a stable patient'.",
      "board_tip": "Severe CAP + shock, no influenza = give hydrocortisone (ATS 2025, conditional). Severe CAP from influenza = no steroids. Non-severe CAP = no steroids regardless."
    },
    {
      "heading": "Outcomes, prognosis, and prevention",
      "minutes": "1-2 min",
      "points": [
        "Mortality tracks severity almost linearly: outpatient CAP <1-2%, hospitalized non-ICU roughly 5-10%, ICU/severe CAP 25-30% or higher with shock. PSI class V carries roughly 27-31% 30-day mortality versus <1% in classes I-II — this is the basis for the outpatient-vs-admit decision. [7]",
        "CURB-65 stratifies similarly: score 0-1 low risk (approximately 1.5% mortality), 2 intermediate, >=3 high risk (>=9-22%) warranting consideration of ICU-level assessment. [8]",
        "In CAPE COD, hydrocortisone in severe CAP produced an absolute 28-day mortality reduction of roughly 6 percentage points — approximately 1 life saved per 17 treated — with more insulin requirement but no excess of hospital-acquired infection. [3]",
        "Prognosis is not just pulmonary: hospitalized CAP triggers cardiovascular events — MI, new AFib, HF decompensation — in a substantial minority, driven by inflammatory plaque destabilization, hypoxemia, and tachycardia. Mortality after CAP hospitalization stays elevated for a year, particularly in older adults with frailty.",

        "Prevention is guideline-level therapy: annual influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccination, and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV21 or PCV20, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23) for all adults >=50 per ACIP 2025; RSV vaccine >=75 and risk-based 60-74. Add smoking cessation and alcohol reduction. [10]"

sections.heading: Physiology: how a bacterium in an alveolus makes a hypoxemic patient
points: Normal alveolus is a 0.5-micron gas-exchange membrane kept dry by tight type I epithelium and active Na+ reabsorption through type II cell ENaC/Na-K-ATPase — this is the surface that pneumonia destroys.

Aspirated Streptococcus pneumoniae reaches the alveolus; its polysaccharide capsule blocks complement C3b deposition and phagocytosis, while pneumolysin (a cholesterol-dependent pore-forming toxin) lyses epithelium and cilia. Bacterial load outruns the resident alveolar macrophage.

Lipoteichoic acid and peptidoglycan ligate TLR2, LPS of gram-negatives ligates TLR4 → MyD88 → NF-kB translocation → IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8. IL-8 recruits neutrophils; IL-6 drives hepatic CRP and fever via prostaglandin E2 at the hypothalamus.

Neutrophil elastase, reactive oxygen species and cytokine-mediated loss of endothelial VE-cadherin junctions cause protein-rich alveolar flooding, and inflammatory exudate inactivates surfactant → alveolar collapse and reduced compliance (the 'consolidation' you percuss and hear as bronchial breath sounds and E-to-A change).

Flooded but still perfused alveoli create true intrapulmonary SHUNT — this is why hypoxemia in dense lobar pneumonia responds poorly to supplemental O2 and why the A-a gradient is widened. Local inflammatory mediators (NO, prostacyclin) blunt hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening the shunt fraction.

Early ABG classically shows hypoxemia with respiratory ALKALOSIS: J-receptor stimulation and cytokines drive tachypnea before CO2 retention. A normal or rising PaCO2 in a tachypneic pneumonia patient signals fatigue — an intubation warning, not reassurance.

When the cytokine response becomes systemic and dysregulated, you get sepsis physiology: nitric oxide/prostacyclin-mediated vasodilation, capillary leak, and mitochondrial dysfunction → lactate elevation and organ failure. CAP is the single most common cause of sepsis. [9]
sections.mechanism: Everything downstream — hypoxemia refractory to O2, the neutrophilic exudate, the fever and CRP, and septic shock — is one pathway: pathogen recognition receptors → NF-kB → cytokine-driven neutrophil influx and endothelial/epithelial barrier failure. Antibiotics remove the trigger; corticosteroids blunt the NF-kB-driven amplification; oxygen and PEEP recruit the flooded units.
sections.teaching_pearl: Bacteremic pneumococcal pneumonia with a widened A-a gradient and refractory hypoxemia is shunt, not V/Q mismatch — putting the patient on 100% FiO2 with minimal PaO2 response is a physiologic diagnosis, not equipment failure.
sections.board_tip: Sputum Gram stain with lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci plus neutrophils = pneumococcus. Elderly patient with hyponatremia, diarrhea, transaminitis and a low-grade relative bradycardia = Legionella — get the urinary antigen.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and site-of-care: the two decisions that change everything
points: Definition is clinical + radiographic: compatible symptoms (cough, fever, dyspnea, pleuritic pain) PLUS a new infiltrate. IDSA/ATS 2019 does not accept a purely clinical diagnosis. [2]
CXR misses up to a quarter of infiltrates in obese or dehydrated patients; CT and lung ultrasound are more sensitive, and ATS 2025 formally addresses lung US as a diagnostic modality. [1]

Site of care is the highest-impact decision (it drives cost and mortality). Use a validated score plus clinical judgment: the 2019 guideline PREFERS the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) over CURB-65 because PSI was validated to identify low-risk outpatients. [2,7,8]

Severe CAP = 1 major criterion (mechanical ventilation or vasopressors) OR >=3 minor criteria (RR >=30, PaO2/FiO2 <=250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, uremia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension requiring aggressive fluids). This label determines microbiology testing, steroid consideration, and duration. [2]

Microbiologic testing is TARGETED, not reflexive: sputum culture and blood cultures for severe CAP, for patients being empirically treated for MRSA or Pseudomonas, or for those with prior isolation of those organisms. Add Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigen in severe CAP. [2]

HCAP is dead — the 2019 guideline eliminated the category. Do not broaden coverage because someone came from a nursing home; assess INDIVIDUAL risk factors for MRSA and Pseudomonas (prior respiratory isolation, recent IV antibiotics, structural lung disease, hospitalization with parenteral antibiotics in 90 days). [2]
Procalcitonin should NOT be used to decide whether to START antibiotics in suspected CAP — a low value does not exclude bacterial pneumonia. [2]

In hypotension or lactate >=4, this is septic shock physiology: lactate, cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, norepinephrine first-line for fluid-refractory hypotension. [9]
sections.teaching_pearl: If the patient does not look like the score, believe your eyes. PSI weights age heavily and will under-call a hypoxemic 40-year-old; CURB-65 has no oxygenation variable at all.
sections.board_tip: A patient sick enough for pressors or a ventilator is severe CAP by definition — no minor criteria counting needed. That single fact unlocks the steroid and microbiology questions.

sections.heading: Empiric antibiotics: pick the pathogen, not the setting
points: Outpatient, no comorbidities (IDSA/ATS 2019, unchanged by ATS 2025): amoxicillin 1 g TID or doxycycline. A macrolide (azithromycin) is first-line ONLY where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25%. [1,2]

Outpatient WITH comorbidities (chronic heart, lung, liver, or kidney disease; diabetes; alcohol use disorder; malignancy; asplenia): beta-lactam (amoxicillin-clavulanate or cefpodoxime/cefuroxime) PLUS a macrolide or doxycycline, or monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin). [2]
Inpatient non-severe: beta-lactam (ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, ampicillin-sulbactam, or ceftaroline) PLUS a macrolide, OR respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy. [2]
Severe CAP: beta-lactam PLUS a macrolide, or beta-lactam PLUS a fluoroquinolone — combination therapy is the standard; do not use fluoroquinolone monotherapy in the ICU patient. [2]

MRSA coverage (vancomycin or linezolid) and antipseudomonal coverage (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, meropenem) ONLY for patients with the specific risk factors above — then obtain cultures and DE-ESCALATE at 48 hours if negative. [2]
Anaerobic coverage is NOT routinely added for suspected aspiration pneumonia; reserve it for lung abscess or empyema. [2]

Influenza-positive CAP still gets antibacterials plus oseltamivir — bacterial co-infection (pneumococcus, S. aureus) is what kills. This is precisely where the 2025 society split lives: ATS made recommendations about withholding/stopping antibiotics in patients with positive viral assays, and IDSA declined to endorse those 2 recommendations while accepting the other 8. Teach the disagreement, not a false consensus. [1]
sections.mechanism: Beta-lactams bind transpeptidases (PBPs) and kill the extracellular, encapsulated pneumococcus that drives lobar consolidation. Macrolides and doxycycline bind the bacterial ribosome (50S and 30S) and penetrate cells, covering the intracellular atypicals — Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia — that a beta-lactam cannot touch. That is why the answer is a beta-lactam PLUS an atypical agent, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV inhibition) that covers both compartments in one drug.
sections.teaching_pearl: Macrolides may add benefit in severe CAP beyond atypical coverage — they downregulate NF-kB signaling and neutrophil recruitment. That immunomodulatory hypothesis is part of why guidelines favor beta-lactam + macrolide over beta-lactam + fluoroquinolone when the patient is critically ill.
sections.board_tip: Vancomycin does NOT belong in routine CAP orders. The board stem that earns MRSA coverage says 'prior respiratory culture with MRSA', 'post-influenza cavitary pneumonia', or 'recent IV antibiotics plus severe illness'.

sections.heading: The 2025 ATS update: steroids in and duration down
points: HIGHEST-YIELD CHANGE: ATS 2025 now SUGGESTS corticosteroids in SEVERE CAP — a reversal of the 2019 recommendation against routine steroids. Note the strength honestly: this is a CONDITIONAL recommendation based on LOW-quality evidence, not a strong one. [1,2]
The exception is explicit: do NOT give corticosteroids for influenza pneumonia (signal of harm — impaired viral clearance and increased mortality in observational data). [1]

Evidence base: CAPE COD randomized hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (tapered, 8-14 days) in severe CAP and showed lower 28-day mortality (6.2% vs 11.9%); Torres 2015 showed reduced treatment failure in severe CAP with high inflammatory response (CRP >150). Earlier ESCAPe was neutral, which is why the recommendation is conditional. [3,4]

SECOND CHANGE — DURATION: 3 to 5 days is now conditionally recommended for outpatients with comorbidities and for inpatients with non-severe CAP who reach clinical stability, with a MINIMUM of 3 days. This is shorter than the 2019 'at least 5 days'. [1,2]

Clinical stability must be documented before stopping: afebrile, HR <100, RR <24, SBP >=90, SpO2 >=90% on room air, able to take oral intake, normal mentation. If not stable at day 3, do not stop. [1]

Trial support for short courses: Uranga 2016 (5 days guided by stability, non-inferior) and the PTC trial (Dinh 2021 — 3 days of beta-lactam non-inferior to 8 in hospitalized non-severe CAP who were stable at day 3). [5,6]

Do not extend antibiotics for a persistent infiltrate. Radiographic clearing lags clinical recovery by weeks; follow-up imaging is for suspected malignancy or non-resolving pneumonia, not for deciding to continue therapy. [2]
sections.mechanism: Glucocorticoids diffuse in, bind the cytosolic glucocorticoid receptor, and both transrepress NF-kB/AP-1 (cutting IL-6, IL-8, TNF transcription) and induce IkB and annexin A1 — reducing neutrophil influx and capillary leak in the alveolus. That is exactly the amplification loop driving hypoxemia and shock in severe CAP. In influenza, the same immunosuppression blunts antiviral T-cell responses and prolongs viral replication, which is why the drug that helps in bacterial severe CAP hurts here.
sections.teaching_pearl: The stability criteria are the real teaching point: short-course therapy is safe because it is CONDITIONAL on the patient having responded. 'Three days' is not a blanket rule — it is 'three days plus a stable patient'.
sections.board_tip: Severe CAP + shock, no influenza = give hydrocortisone (ATS 2025, conditional). Severe CAP from influenza = no steroids. Non-severe CAP = no steroids regardless.

sections.heading: Outcomes, prognosis, and prevention
points: Mortality tracks severity almost linearly: outpatient CAP <1-2%, hospitalized non-ICU roughly 5-10%, ICU/severe CAP 25-30% or higher with shock. PSI class V carries roughly 27-31% 30-day mortality versus <1% in classes I-II — this is the basis for the outpatient-vs-admit decision. [7]
CURB-65 stratifies similarly: score 0-1 low risk (approximately 1.5% mortality), 2 intermediate, >=3 high risk (>=9-22%) warranting consideration of ICU-level assessment. [8]

In CAPE COD, hydrocortisone in severe CAP produced an absolute 28-day mortality reduction of roughly 6 percentage points — approximately 1 life saved per 17 treated — with more insulin requirement but no excess of hospital-acquired infection. [3]

Prognosis is not just pulmonary: hospitalized CAP triggers cardiovascular events — MI, new AFib, HF decompensation — in a substantial minority, driven by inflammatory plaque destabilization, hypoxemia, and tachycardia. Mortality after CAP hospitalization stays elevated for a year, particularly in older adults with frailty.

Drivers of bad outcome are mostly host factors: age, functional dependence, immunosuppression, multilobar involvement, bacteremia, initial shock, and delay to appropriate antibiotics — the last is the only one you fully control. [9]

Prevention is guideline-level therapy: annual influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccination, and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV21 or PCV20, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23) for all adults >=50 per ACIP 2025; RSV vaccine >=75 and risk-based 60-74. Add smoking cessation and alcohol reduction. [10]
sections.teaching_pearl: Failure to improve by 72 hours should trigger a differential, not an antibiotic escalation: empyema or abscess (get a CT and consider thoracentesis), resistant or unexpected organism, obstructing lesion, or a CAP mimic — organizing pneumonia, PE with infarct, HF, or vasculitis.
sections.board_tip: New pleural effusion with failure to improve = sample it. pH <7.20, glucose <60, LDH >1000, or positive Gram stain means complicated effusion/empyema requiring drainage — antibiotics alone will not cure it.

summary_points: CAP hypoxemia is intrapulmonary SHUNT from cytokine-driven alveolar flooding and surfactant inactivation, so it responds poorly to supplemental oxygen — and a normalizing PaCO2 in a tachypneic patient is a sign of fatigue, not improvement.

Severity determines everything: use PSI (preferred) or CURB-65 for site of care, and define severe CAP as 1 major criterion (ventilation or vasopressors) or >=3 minor criteria — that label drives cultures, combination therapy, and steroid consideration. [2]

Empiric therapy pairs a beta-lactam (extracellular pneumococcus) with a macrolide or doxycycline (intracellular atypicals), or uses a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone; HCAP is retired, so add MRSA or Pseudomonas coverage only for individual risk factors and de-escalate at 48 hours. [1,2]

ATS 2025 now suggests corticosteroids in severe CAP — a conditional, low-certainty recommendation reversing 2019 — with hydrocortisone 200 mg/day per CAPE COD, but explicitly NOT in influenza pneumonia. [1,3]

Duration is shorter: 3-5 days (minimum 3) for outpatients with comorbidities and inpatients with non-severe CAP who reach documented clinical stability, supported by Uranga 2016 and the PTC trial. Never extend antibiotics for a lingering infiltrate. [1,5,6]

Know the society split: IDSA endorsed 8 of 10 ATS 2025 recommendations but declined the 2 on withholding/stopping antibiotics in patients with positive viral assays — there is no single consensus CAP document anymore. [1]

gemini_errors: Defines severe CAP only by '≥3 ATS minor criteria' and omits the major criteria (invasive mechanical ventilation, septic shock requiring vasopressors) — a patient on pressors is severe CAP by definition, and this omission distorts the steroid/microbiology teaching that follows.
CURB-65 blood-pressure criterion written as 'BP <90/60' implies both values are required; the criterion is SBP <90 mmHg OR DBP ≤60 mmHg.

States beta-lactam + macrolide is 'preferred over fluoroquinolone' in severe CAP; IDSA/ATS 2019 lists beta-lactam plus either macrolide or fluoroquinolone as acceptable (only fluoroquinolone MONOtherapy is discouraged) — the preference is observational, not a guideline statement.
Quotes ICU CAP mortality of '20–50%', an upper bound well above contemporary severe-CAP cohorts (~25–30%).
claude_errors: Cites 'Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 International Guidelines' as a source; the recommendations actually quoted (antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, norepinephrine first-line) are SSC 2021 — attributing them to an unverifiable 2026 document is a citation-honesty problem.

'CXR misses up to a quarter of infiltrates in obese or dehydrated patients' — the dehydration mechanism is largely a teaching myth and the quantitative figure derives from CT-comparison studies, not obesity/dehydration-specific data.
judge.why: Both artifacts share the same core framing (2025 ATS update, IDSA's partial non-endorsement, conditional/low-certainty steroids, shorter duration) and both correctly flag the influenza exception and the retirement of HCAP. B is superior on guideline fidelity and teaching value: it gets the full severe-CAP definition (1 major OR ≥3 minor), correctly notes the 2019 preference for PSI over CURB-65, includes the procalcitonin and anaerobic-coverage recommendations, and — critically — anchors its claims to real, correctly summarized primary trials (CAPE COD 6.2% vs 11.9%, Torres 2015, ESCAPe neutrality, Uranga 2016, PTC/Dinh 2021) with accurate numbers, plus clinical-stability criteria that make the 3-day recommendation safe to teach. A's citations are thinner and it commits two substantive teaching errors (incomplete severe-CAP definition, overstated preference for beta-lactam+macrolide in the ICU). A does deserve credit for repeatedly emphasizing the conditional, low-certainty nature of the steroid recommendation, but B does this equally well and adds mechanism, mimics, effusion management, and prevention. B's only real deduction is the questionable 'SSC 2026' attribution.

question.stem:
A 68-year-old woman with COPD is brought to the emergency department for 3 days of fever, productive cough, and worsening dyspnea. In the ED she becomes hypotensive and hypoxic despite fluid resuscitation, requiring norepinephrine and endotracheal intubation for respiratory failure. She is started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin and admitted to the ICU.

Temperature 38.9°C, BP 84/50 mmHg on norepinephrine, HR 118/min, RR 28/min (ventilated), SpO2 92% on FiO2 0.6. Diffuse crackles are heard bilaterally.

Procalcitonin 4.2 ng/mL. Influenza A/B and SARS-CoV-2 PCR are negative. CXR shows bilateral multilobar infiltrates. Blood cultures are pending.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Discontinue antibiotics based on the respiratory viral panel
Plan to stop antibiotics after 3 days of therapy

question.explanation: This patient meets ATS major criteria for severe CAP (septic shock requiring vasopressors and acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation). The ATS 2025 CAP update issues a conditional, low-quality-evidence recommendation FOR adjunctive corticosteroids in severe CAP - a reversal of the 2019 ATS/IDSA guidance against routine steroid use - with the explicit exception of influenza pneumonia, where steroids may worsen outcomes. Influenza PCR here is negative, so the exception does not apply and corticosteroids (e.g., hydrocortisone) should be added to antibiotic therapy [1]. IDSA accepted this recommendation as part of the 8 of 10 statements it endorsed from the 2025 update. Corticosteroids are given as an adjunct to, not a replacement for, antimicrobial therapy in this critically ill patient.

wrong_explanations.why: Empiric oseltamivir is indicated for suspected or confirmed influenza pending or with testing; PCR is already negative, so antiviral therapy adds no benefit and misapplies the influenza-exception logic.
This reflects the superseded 2019 ATS/IDSA position recommending against routine steroids; the 2025 update reverses this specifically for severe CAP without influenza.

This mirrors the two ATS 2025 recommendations on withholding/de-escalating antibiotics with a positive viral assay that IDSA explicitly declined to endorse; stopping antibacterial therapy in a patient with septic shock and multilobar infiltrates is unsafe regardless.

The 3-5 day shortened-duration recommendation applies only after the patient reaches clinical stability (minimum 3 days); this patient remains on vasopressors and mechanical ventilation, so early cessation is premature.

question.difficulty_rationale: Requires recognizing severe CAP by major criteria, applying the newly reversed 2025 corticosteroid recommendation, correctly excluding the influenza carve-out via a negative PCR, and rejecting two closely related distractors drawn from the guideline's contested and misapplied elements.
reasoning_steps: Identify that septic shock requiring vasopressors plus need for mechanical ventilation meets ATS major criteria for severe CAP
Confirm influenza has been excluded by negative PCR, satisfying the exception carve-out for corticosteroid use
Apply the ATS 2025 CAP update's conditional recommendation for adjunctive corticosteroids in severe CAP without influenza
Recognize the patient is not yet clinically stable, so the shortened antibiotic-duration rule does not yet apply
Eliminate the distractor of stopping antibiotics based on viral testing, a recommendation IDSA specifically declined to endorse

talk.key_point: In severe CAP without influenza, the ATS 2025 CAP update (IDSA-endorsed) conditionally recommends adjunctive corticosteroids, reversing the 2019 stance against routine steroid use.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Severe Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Adjunctive Corticosteroids (ATS 2025 Update)

board_pearls: Corticosteroids attenuate the dysregulated hyperinflammatory response in severe CAP, potentially limiting progression to ARDS and shock.
ATS 2025 conditionally recommends corticosteroids in severe CAP EXCEPT influenza pneumonia - IDSA accepted this specific recommendation as part of its 8 of 10 endorsed statements [1].
The discriminator versus the 2019 recommendation is severity: ATS major criteria (vasopressor-dependent shock or invasive mechanical ventilation) trigger steroid consideration, not mild-moderate CAP.
This builds on trial evidence (e.g., hydrocortisone in severe CAP/ARDS trials such as CAPE COD) informing the conditional, low-certainty guideline language [3].

The classic trap is either clinging to the outdated 2019 anti-steroid stance, or de-escalating/stopping antibiotics based on a positive viral assay - a recommendation IDSA explicitly rejected in the 2025 update.
teaching_points: Severity in CAP is defined by ATS major criteria (septic shock needing vasopressors, respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation), not CURB-65 alone.
The ATS 2025 CAP update is contested: IDSA endorsed 8 of 10 recommendations but rejected the 2 concerning antibiotic decisions based on positive viral assays.
Shortened antibiotic duration (3-5 days) requires the patient to first reach clinical stability, with a minimum of 3 days regardless of stability.
summary_points: In severe CAP (ATS major criteria) without influenza, add adjunctive corticosteroids per the ATS 2025 update, which IDSA has endorsed.

talk.title: Severe Community-Acquired Pneumonia in the ICU: Who Gets Steroids?
talk.subtitle: Applying the ATS 2025 CAP update — and the influenza exception
guideline_sources: ATS 2025 CAP Update (IDSA did not endorse in full)
IDSA/ATS 2019 Community-Acquired Pneumonia Guideline
Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026

references.source: An Official ATS Clinical Practice Guideline Update: Treatment of Adults with Community-Acquired Pneumonia
Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-acquired Pneumonia (Metlay et al., AJRCCM 2019;200:e45)
CAPE COD trial: Hydrocortisone in Severe Community-Acquired Pneumonia (Dequin et al., N Engl J Med 2023)
Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock

question.stem:
A 68-year-old woman is evaluated in the ICU 8 hours after admission for community-acquired pneumonia that began 3 days earlier with fever, productive cough, and progressive dyspnea in early February. She has HTN and T2DM. She has had no hospitalization, no IV antibiotics, and no prior MRSA or Pseudomonas isolation. Worsening hypoxemia required intubation on arrival; ceftriaxone and azithromycin were started within 1 hour after blood and sputum cultures were obtained.

Temperature 38.9 C, BP 112/68 mm Hg without vasopressors, HR 104/min, RR 20/min on the ventilator, SpO2 94% on FiO2 0.50 with PEEP 8 cm H2O. Examination shows bibasilar crackles.

Leukocytes 16,800/uL, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin 4.2 ng/mL, PaO2/FiO2 168. Nasopharyngeal PCR is negative for influenza A/B and SARS-CoV-2; urinary pneumococcal antigen is positive. CXR shows bilateral lower lobe consolidation.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation: This patient has SEVERE CAP by an ATS major criterion (need for invasive mechanical ventilation), with pneumococcal etiology and a negative influenza PCR. The ATS 2025 CAP update SUGGESTS systemic corticosteroids for patients hospitalized with severe CAP, EXCEPT when influenza pneumonia is present (conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). This is an explicit REVERSAL of IDSA/ATS 2019, which recommended against routine corticosteroids in CAP absent refractory shock. The recommendation is driven largely by CAPE COD (NEJM 2023), in which hydrocortisone 200 mg/day started within 24 hours of severe CAP reduced 28-day mortality; benefit is greatest when steroids are given EARLY, making this the appropriate next step now rather than after further deterioration. Evidence status matters: this is a conditional, low-certainty recommendation, and IDSA declined to endorse the ATS 2025 document in full — though its objections concerned the two recommendations about antibiotics in patients with positive viral assays, not the corticosteroid statement. Note that steroids here are indicated for severe CAP itself, not for vasopressor-refractory shock (the Surviving Sepsis 2026 indication), which this normotensive patient does not have. Antibiotic therapy is already guideline-concordant: a beta-lactam plus macrolide is recommended empiric coverage for severe inpatient CAP, and this patient has no individual risk factors for MRSA or Pseudomonas (no prior isolation, no IV antibiotics or hospitalization in 90 days), so broadening is not indicated — the HCAP category was eliminated in 2019. Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 testing are negative, removing both the antiviral indication and the influenza exception to steroid use.

wrong_explanations.why: Influenza A/B PCR is negative and pneumococcal antigen is positive; empiric oseltamivir is not indicated. Its relevance here is inverted — a POSITIVE influenza test would have been the reason to WITHHOLD corticosteroids under ATS 2025.

MRSA and Pseudomonas coverage requires individual risk factors (prior respiratory isolation, or hospitalization plus IV antibiotics within 90 days). She has none. Broadening based on ICU admission alone reflects the retired HCAP concept eliminated in 2019.

Severe CAP requires combination therapy: beta-lactam PLUS macrolide (or a respiratory fluoroquinolone). Dropping azithromycin removes atypical coverage and the macrolide's observed mortality benefit in severe disease; de-escalation would occur only later with a defined pathogen and clinical stability.

Fluoroquinolone monotherapy is an acceptable alternative empiric regimen, but switching an appropriately treated, culture-pending patient adds QT and tendon/CNS risk without benefit. It also fails to address the actual gap in management — the missing adjunctive corticosteroid.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must classify the pneumonia as severe by a major criterion, recognize that current antibiotics are already guideline-concordant, verify absence of MRSA/Pseudomonas risk, and apply a 2025 recommendation that reversed prior guidance while checking its single exception.
reasoning_steps: Classify severity: invasive mechanical ventilation is an ATS major criterion, so this is severe CAP.
Verify the empiric regimen is already correct: beta-lactam plus macrolide with no individual MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors, so broadening or switching adds nothing.
Recall the ATS 2025 update: corticosteroids are suggested in severe CAP (conditional, low certainty), reversing IDSA/ATS 2019.
Check the exception: influenza pneumonia contraindicates adjunctive steroids — influenza PCR is negative here, and pneumococcal antigen is positive.
Conclude that early (within 24 hours) hydrocortisone is the next step, distinct from the refractory-shock steroid indication, which this normotensive patient does not meet.

talk.key_point: In severe CAP requiring mechanical ventilation or vasopressors, add systemic corticosteroids early unless influenza pneumonia is present — a conditional, low-certainty ATS 2025 recommendation reversing 2019 guidance. [1]

abim_classification.specific_topic: Severe community-acquired pneumonia: adjunctive corticosteroids and empiric coverage

board_pearls: Corticosteroids in severe CAP blunt the dysregulated inflammatory response driving ARDS-like lung injury and shock; benefit depends on EARLY initiation (within 24 hours), which is why the decision is made at admission, not after deterioration. [3]

ATS 2025 SUGGESTS corticosteroids for severe CAP except influenza pneumonia — conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence — reversing the IDSA/ATS 2019 recommendation against routine steroids. [1,2]

The discriminator versus broadening antibiotics: MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage requires INDIVIDUAL risk factors (prior respiratory isolation, or hospitalization plus IV antibiotics within 90 days); ICU admission alone is not one, since HCAP was eliminated in 2019. [2]

CAPE COD (NEJM 2023) showed hydrocortisone 200 mg/day reduced 28-day mortality in severe CAP; ATS severity criteria (2 major: mechanical ventilation, vasopressors; or 3+ minor) define eligibility. [1,3]

Trap: giving oseltamivir or withholding steroids on the assumption of viral pneumonia. A POSITIVE influenza test is the reason to withhold steroids; a negative test with positive pneumococcal antigen supports giving them. [1]
teaching_points: Severe CAP is defined by ATS criteria: either major criterion (invasive mechanical ventilation or vasopressor-requiring septic shock) or 3 or more minor criteria (RR >=30, PaO2/FiO2 <=250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, uremia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension requiring fluids).

There is no longer a single consensus CAP guideline: IDSA declined to endorse ATS 2025 in full, objecting to the two recommendations on antibiotics in patients with positive viral assays; teach the split rather than a unified voice. [1]

ATS 2025 also conditionally shortens therapy to 3-5 days (minimum 3) for outpatients with comorbidities and inpatients with non-severe CAP who reach clinical stability — this shortening does not apply to severe CAP as presented here. [1]
summary_points: Intubated, non-influenza severe CAP on appropriate beta-lactam plus macrolide: the missing element is early adjunctive corticosteroid, not broader or different antibiotics. [1,3]

gemini_errors: Reference 3 is mislabeled as 'Dexamethasone in Patients with ARDS Associated with COVID-19' while the DOI/URL (NEJMoa2215145) and parenthetical refer to CAPE COD (hydrocortisone, Dequin et al.) — a misattributed citation conflating two unrelated trials

Board pearl frames the evidence as 'hydrocortisone in severe CAP/ARDS trials such as CAPE COD,' incorrectly lumping CAPE COD with COVID/ARDS steroid trials rather than its actual severe-CAP population (which excluded influenza)

States as fact that IDSA 'accepted this recommendation as part of the 8 of 10 statements it endorsed' and labels the update flatly 'IDSA-endorsed' — an overstated, specific endorsement claim presented without hedging

Asserts empiric oseltamivir 'adds no benefit' solely because a nasopharyngeal PCR is negative in a ventilated, shocked patient, where lower-tract testing and continued empiric antiviral therapy are often warranted during influenza season
claude_errors: Lists and cites a "Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 (SCCM/ESICM)" guideline; the extant SSC document is 2021 — the cited year/source is not a verifiable guideline and functions as a fabricated citation

Characterizes the SSC steroid indication as 'vasopressor-refractory shock'; SSC actually suggests low-dose corticosteroids for septic shock with an ongoing vasopressor requirement (e.g., norepinephrine ≥0.25 mcg/kg/min for ≥4 h), which is a lower threshold than 'refractory'

Treats a single negative nasopharyngeal influenza PCR as definitively excluding influenza in an intubated patient in February; in severe/ventilated CAP, lower respiratory tract sampling is advised and empiric oseltamivir is often continued when suspicion is high
judge.why: Both artifacts get the core teaching point right (ATS 2025 conditional, low-certainty recommendation for adjunctive corticosteroids in severe CAP with an influenza carve-out, reversing 2019) and both correctly apply ATS major severity criteria. A is superior in teaching value and internal rigor: its vignette isolates the severe-CAP steroid indication (intubation, normotensive, lactate normal) from the separate septic-shock steroid indication, and it adds high-yield discriminators (beta-lactam+macrolide for severe CAP, individual MRSA/Pseudomonas risk factors, retirement of HCAP, correct minor-criteria list, appropriately hedged strength of evidence). B's vignette is confounded because vasopressor-dependent shock would trigger corticosteroids under sepsis guidance regardless of the CAP update, and B commits a clear citation-honesty error by titling the CAPE COD reference as a COVID-19 ARDS dexamethasone trial and later blending the two literatures. A's principal flaw is citing a 'Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026' document that does not exist as described, plus a mischaracterization of the SSC steroid threshold — real but peripheral to the answer, whereas B's misattribution touches the pivotal trial itself.

talk.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
talk.subtitle: Insulin deficiency, unopposed lipolysis, and the anion gap acidosis it produces — endocrine/critical care chalk talk
guideline_sources: ADA Standards of Care 2025
ADA/EASD Consensus Report on Hyperglycemic Crises 2024 (Diabetes Care)

references.source: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults with Diabetes: A Consensus Report
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025
Hyperglycemic Crises in Adult Patients with Diabetes (Position Statement)
FDA Drug Safety Communication: SGLT2 inhibitors and ketoacidosis

sections.heading: Physiology & Pathophysiology — Why Ketones Accumulate
points: DKA = absolute (or severe relative) insulin deficiency plus excess counterregulatory hormones (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, GH). Insulin normally suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase in adipocytes; without it, unrestrained lipolysis floods the liver with free fatty acids.

Glucagon excess (unopposed by insulin) drives hepatic carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1) activity up, shuttling those fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation → acetyl-CoA → hepatic ketogenesis (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate). This is a normal starvation pathway pushed into pathologic overdrive.

Insulin deficiency also unleashes hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis while peripheral glucose uptake in muscle/fat is blocked → severe hyperglycemia (usually >250 mg/dL, though euglycemic DKA occurs, see below).

Glucose above the renal threshold (~180 mg/dL) causes osmotic diuresis → profound total-body water and electrolyte losses (Na, K, phosphate, magnesium) despite a normal or even elevated serum K on initial labs, because acidosis and insulinopenia shift K out of cells even as total-body K is depleted.

Ketoacids (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate) are strong acids that consume serum bicarbonate buffering capacity → high anion gap metabolic acidosis; Kussmaul respirations are the respiratory compensation (blowing off CO2 to raise pH).
sections.mechanism: The entire syndrome is one hormonal switch flipped the wrong way: insulin off, glucagon/catecholamines on. That single imbalance simultaneously turns on lipolysis, ketogenesis, gluconeogenesis, and osmotic diuresis — every downstream lab abnormality traces back to it.
sections.teaching_pearl: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) can precipitate euglycemic DKA — the drug blocks renal glucose reabsorption so serum glucose stays deceptively low (<250 mg/dL) even while ketogenesis rages, because insulinopenia/relative deficiency and glucagon excess still occur. Perioperative fasting, low-carb diets, and illness are classic triggers [4].
sections.board_tip: Classic triggers to memorize: the 5 I's — Infection, Infarction (MI), Insulin non-adherence, Intoxication (alcohol/cocaine), and Iatrogenic (SGLT2i, steroids, antipsychotics). New-onset T1DM presenting as DKA is also common in adults, not just kids.

sections.heading: Clinical Findings & Workup
points: Diagnostic triad: hyperglycemia (usually >250 mg/dL, lower or normal in euglycemic DKA), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <18 mEq/L), and ketonemia/ketonuria (beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L or moderate-large urine ketones) [1,3].
Exam: Kussmaul respirations, fruity (acetone) breath, diffuse abdominal pain/vomiting (can mimic an acute abdomen), dehydration, tachycardia, and altered mental status if severe.

Labs: BMP/CMP (Na, K, bicarbonate, BUN/Cr), venous blood gas (VBG is sufficient — arterial not required), serum or urine ketones, anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3), calculated/corrected sodium (add 1.6 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL glucose above 100), and a search for the precipitant (CBC with differential, UA, blood cultures, CXR, troponin, lipase as indicated).
Severity grading (ADA/EASD 2024) uses pH, bicarbonate, and mental status to stratify mild/moderate/severe — this determines insulin route and ICU-level monitoring needs [1].
sections.teaching_pearl: Don't be fooled by a 'normal' or high potassium on initial BMP — acidosis drives K out of cells via H+/K+ exchange even though total-body K is markedly depleted from osmotic diuresis and vomiting. Never give insulin before confirming K is not already low.
sections.board_tip: Corrected sodium is a board favorite: true hyponatremia from hyperglycemia's osmotic pull of water out of cells must be distinguished from a 'real' sodium disturbance — always calculate it before interpreting Na level.

sections.heading: Treatment — Fluids, Insulin, Potassium, and the Transition Off
points: Fluids first: isotonic saline (0.9% NaCl) 15-20 mL/kg (roughly 1-1.5 L) in the first hour to restore intravascular volume and improve renal perfusion, which itself lowers glucose by improving urinary clearance and reduces counterregulatory hormone drive [1,2].

Check potassium before insulin. If K <3.3 mEq/L, hold insulin and replete K first — insulin drives K intracellularly via Na-K-ATPase stimulation and can precipitate life-threatening hypokalemia and arrhythmia. If K 3.3-5.3, add 20-30 mEq K to each liter of fluid. If K >5.3, hold K repletion and recheck [1,3].

Insulin: regular insulin IV infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hr (or 0.14 unit/kg/hr without a bolus) is the mainstay per ADA/EASD 2024 [1]. Mechanism: insulin shuts off hepatic ketogenesis (suppresses CPT-1/lipolysis) and gluconeogenesis, and drives peripheral glucose uptake — this resolves the acidosis, not just the hyperglycemia. Continue the infusion until anion gap closes and ketosis resolves, not just until glucose normalizes.

Add dextrose (D5 or D10) to IV fluids once glucose falls to ~200-250 mg/dL, while continuing the insulin infusion — this allows insulin to keep suppressing ketogenesis without causing hypoglycemia (glucose is the target you titrate around, but ketone/gap closure is the actual therapeutic endpoint).

Bicarbonate is NOT routinely recommended (only considered if pH <6.9) — the acidosis corrects as ketogenesis shuts off and is largely self-limited with fluids/insulin; bicarbonate can worsen hypokalemia and paradoxical CNS acidosis [1,3].

Transition to subcutaneous insulin only once the gap has closed, bicarbonate ≥18, and the patient can eat — overlap the first subQ dose with the IV infusion by 1-2 hours (subQ insulin takes time to reach therapeutic levels) to avoid rebound ketoacidosis [1].
sections.mechanism: Insulin's job in DKA is fundamentally anti-lipolytic and anti-ketogenic — it re-suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase and hepatic CPT-1, cutting off the fatty-acid supply to ketogenesis. Correcting glucose is almost a side effect; the true endpoint of therapy is anion gap closure, which is why you keep the insulin drip running (with dextrose backup) even after glucose normalizes.
sections.teaching_pearl: If a patient is on an SGLT2 inhibitor and presents with euglycemic DKA, treat identically (fluids, insulin, K, dextrose once glucose falls) — do not withhold insulin just because glucose looks reassuring; the ketogenesis is the disease, not the glucose number [4].
sections.board_tip: Two board pitfalls: (1) starting insulin before checking/repleting a low K → arrhythmia; (2) stopping the insulin drip as soon as glucose normalizes without ensuring the anion gap has closed → rebound DKA. Insulin infusion continues until the gap closes, with dextrose added to prevent hypoglycemia.

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: Adult DKA mortality is low (<1%) in modern management when treated per protocol at experienced centers, but rises sharply with age, severe acidosis (pH <7.0), and coma on presentation [1].

Cerebral edema is the feared complication and is largely a pediatric/young-adult phenomenon (incidence <1% but mortality 20-50% when it occurs) — thought to relate to overly rapid osmotic shifts, so fluid correction is more conservative in children.

Recurrent DKA is most often driven by insulin non-adherence (often due to cost/access) or undiagnosed precipitating infection — addressing the underlying driver is as important as the acute metabolic correction [1].
sections.teaching_pearl: Every DKA admission is an opportunity to identify and fix the precipitant (missed insulin doses, new SGLT2i, infection, first presentation of T1DM) — treating the acidosis without addressing the trigger guarantees a bounce-back.

summary_points: DKA is fundamentally an insulin-deficiency/glucagon-excess state: unrestrained lipolysis feeds hepatic ketogenesis via CPT-1, producing the anion gap acidosis — hyperglycemia is a parallel effect, not the core problem.
Diagnosis requires the triad: hyperglycemia (or euglycemia with SGLT2i), high anion gap metabolic acidosis, and ketonemia/ketonuria — always calculate the corrected sodium and anion gap.

Treatment sequence matters: fluids first, check/replete potassium before starting insulin, then IV regular insulin infusion (0.1 unit/kg/hr) with dextrose added once glucose falls to ~200-250, continued until the anion gap closes — not until glucose normalizes [1].
Bicarbonate is reserved for pH <6.9 only; routine use is not guideline-recommended and can worsen hypokalemia [1,3].
Most common pitfalls: starting insulin with an undiscovered low potassium, and stopping the insulin drip too early (glucose-normal but gap still open) causing rebound ketoacidosis.
SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycemic DKA — a normal glucose does not rule out DKA in a patient on these agents [4].

visual_memory_card.top_left: No insulin → unopposed lipolysis feeds hepatic ketogenesis
visual_memory_card.top_right: Hyperglycemia + high anion gap acidosis + ketonemia, Kussmaul breathing
visual_memory_card.bottom_left: VBG + BMP + beta-hydroxybutyrate + anion gap + corrected Na
visual_memory_card.bottom_right: IV fluids, then insulin infusion (shuts off ketogenesis) + K repletion, add dextrose

sections.heading: The Physiology: Why Absent Insulin Makes Acid
points: DKA requires TWO hormonal events: near-absolute insulin deficiency PLUS counterregulatory excess (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, growth hormone). Insulin resistance alone (T2DM) usually does not do it — you need enough insulinopenia to release the brake on fat.

In adipose tissue, insulin normally activates Akt → phosphodiesterase-3B → falls in cAMP/PKA → hormone-sensitive lipase and ATGL stay dephosphorylated and quiet. Remove insulin and add catecholamines, and lipolysis runs wide open: a flood of free fatty acids (FFAs) and glycerol reaches the liver.

In the hepatocyte, glucagon dominance drops malonyl-CoA, which disinhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1) — the gate into mitochondria. FFAs pour into β-oxidation and generate acetyl-CoA far faster than the TCA cycle can consume it (oxaloacetate is being siphoned into gluconeogenesis).

Overflow acetyl-CoA is condensed by HMG-CoA synthase into acetoacetate, most of which is reduced to β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) by mitochondrial NADH. In DKA the BHB:acetoacetate ratio is typically 3–10:1 — which is exactly why urine nitroprusside strips, which detect acetoacetate and acetone but NOT BHB, understate severity. [1]

BHB and acetoacetate are strong organic acids fully dissociated at physiologic pH. Their H+ titrates bicarbonate; the unmeasured conjugate base is the anion gap. Respiratory compensation gives Kussmaul breathing; volatile acetone gives the fruity breath.

In parallel, glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis + loss of GLUT4-mediated uptake drive glucose above the ~180 mg/dL renal threshold → osmotic diuresis. Classic deficits: water ~100 mL/kg, Na ~7–10 mEq/kg, K ~3–5 mEq/kg, phosphate ~1 mmol/kg. Vomiting from ketosis and gastroparesis compounds the loss. [6]

Key trap in the physiology: serum K is often normal or HIGH at presentation despite a large total-body deficit, because insulinopenia, hyperosmolality, and acidemia all shift K out of cells. Insulin will unmask the true deficit within hours.

summary_points: DKA is a fat disease, not a sugar disease: insulinopenia plus glucagon excess disinhibits hormone-sensitive lipase and CPT-1, flooding the liver with FFAs that overflow into β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate — strong acids that consume bicarbonate and open the anion gap.

Per the 2024 ADA/EASD consensus, diagnose with glucose ≥200 mg/dL (or known diabetes) + BHB ≥3.0 mmol/L (or ketones ≥2+) + bicarbonate ≤18 and/or pH ≤7.3; grade severity by pH/bicarbonate, not mental status, and follow BHB rather than urine ketones.

Treat in order: isotonic fluid first (balanced crystalloid suggested over 0.9% saline — conditional, limited-quality evidence, supported by SCOPE-DKA and the SMART DKA subgroup), then insulin 0.1 U/kg/h, and check potassium before insulin — hold insulin if K <3.3 mmol/L.

Add dextrose when glucose <250 mg/dL and keep insulin running until BHB <0.6 mmol/L with pH >7.3 or bicarbonate ≥18; overlap subcutaneous basal insulin 1.5–2 hours before stopping the drip or the patient rebounds.
Mild-to-moderate uncomplicated DKA can be managed with protocolized subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin outside the ICU — an evidence-based alternative endorsed in 2024, not a shortcut.

Euglycemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors is the classic miss: check BHB regardless of glucose, run insulin with dextrose, and hold the drug 3–4 days before surgery or during acute illness. Death in DKA comes from the precipitant and from recurrence driven by insulin access — address both before discharge.

gemini_errors: States that the ADA/EASD 2024 severity grading 'uses pH, bicarbonate, and mental status' and cites ref [1] — the 2024 consensus specifically REMOVED mental status from severity criteria and grades mild/moderate/severe by pH and bicarbonate alone

Presents the diagnostic triad with hyperglycemia 'usually >250 mg/dL' citing the 2024 consensus [1,3]; the 2024 report lowered the glucose criterion to ≥200 mg/dL (or a known history of diabetes), so the threshold is attributed to a source that does not support it

Potassium bands (3.3–5.3 mEq/L, 20–30 mEq/L replacement) and the bicarbonate threshold of pH <6.9 are 2009-era numbers attributed in part to the 2024 consensus [1], which uses 3.3–5.0 mmol/L, 10–20 mEq/L, and pH <7.0
Cerebral edema mortality quoted as 20–50%; contemporary pediatric data place case fatality around 20–25% (with additional neurologic morbidity), so the upper bound is overstated

Omits/contradicts current practice by stating IV regular insulin infusion is 'the mainstay per ADA/EASD 2024' without noting the consensus endorses protocolized subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin for mild–moderate uncomplicated DKA
Resolution endpoint given only as anion-gap closure/HCO3 ≥18; 2024 defines resolution by BHB <0.6 mmol/L plus pH >7.30 or HCO3 ≥18, and explicitly prefers BHB over the gap
claude_errors: Labels the dilutional/translocational hyponatremia of hyperglycemia as 'pseudohyponatremia'; pseudohyponatremia is a distinct laboratory artifact from hyperlipidemia/hyperproteinemia

SCOPE-DKA is cited as Crit Care Med; it was published in Intensive Care Medicine (2021), and faster ketoacidosis resolution was a secondary/24-hour outcome rather than the primary endpoint — the trial's framing is slightly stronger than the data
Fluid rate of 500–1000 mL/h is equated to '10–15 mL/kg/h', which is arithmetically off for an average adult (≈7–14 mL/kg/h)
Rising DKA hospitalization rates in adults <45 are attributed to ADA Standards of Care 2025 [2]; that epidemiologic claim derives from CDC/surveillance data, not the Standards
judge.why: Both are pedagogically strong and share the same correct core physiology (insulinopenia + glucagon → HSL/CPT-1 disinhibition → ketogenesis) and the same core management sequence. B is materially more faithful to the 2024 ADA/EASD consensus it claims as its anchor: correct new diagnostic thresholds (glucose ≥200 or known diabetes, BHB ≥3.0, HCO3 ≤18/pH ≤7.3), correct severity grading by acid-base with mental status removed, BHB-based monitoring and resolution criteria (BHB <0.6), correct K bands and bicarbonate threshold (pH <7.0), and appropriately hedged 'conditional/low-quality' language for balanced crystalloids with accurately identified supporting trials (SMART/SALT-ED subgroup, Umpierrez 2004 SC lispro). A is safe and internally coherent but is essentially the 2009 position statement while citing the 2024 consensus for it, and it makes one outright wrong guideline claim (mental status as a 2024 severity criterion). A's citation honesty is therefore weaker even though its clinical advice would not harm a patient. B's residual errors are nomenclature and reference-metadata nits.

question.stem:
A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is admitted to the ICU for diabetic ketoacidosis after presenting with polyuria, vomiting, and Kussmaul breathing. She was started on IV normal saline and a continuous IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr. Potassium was 4.2 mEq/L at admission and has been repleted per protocol. After 6 hours of therapy, her blood glucose has fallen from 480 mg/dL to 175 mg/dL, but she remains tachypneic.

Temperature 37.0°C, BP 108/68 mm Hg, HR 96/min, RR 24/min, SpO2 99% on room air. She appears mildly uncomfortable; mucous membranes are dry.

Repeat labs: glucose 175 mg/dL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, anion gap 19, beta-hydroxybutyrate elevated, potassium 3.9 mEq/L.

The bedside nurse asks whether the insulin infusion should be stopped now that the glucose goal has been reached. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue the insulin infusion
Administer sodium bicarbonate to correct the anion gap
Decrease the insulin infusion rate to prevent hypoglycemia
Discontinue the infusion and start subcutaneous insulin
Discontinue the infusion and repeat labs in 4 hours

question.explanation: Per the ADA/AACE Hyperglycemic Crises Consensus Statement (2009, reaffirmed in ADA Standards of Care 2025), resolution of DKA is defined biochemically by closure of the anion gap and normalization of bicarbonate/pH — not by normalization of glucose. Glucose typically falls faster than ketoacidosis resolves because insulin's effect on glucose uptake outpaces its effect on suppressing lipolysis and ketogenesis. This patient's glucose has reached 175 mg/dL, but her anion gap (19) and bicarbonate (14) remain abnormal and beta-hydroxybutyrate is still elevated, indicating active ketoacidosis. The guideline-recommended action once glucose reaches approximately 200 mg/dL is to add dextrose (D5 or D5-1/2NS) to the IV fluids while continuing the insulin infusion (the rate may be reduced modestly, typically to 0.02-0.05 units/kg/hr) to prevent hypoglycemia while sustaining ketone clearance until the anion gap normalizes. Stopping insulin at this point removes the drug that is actively suppressing ketogenesis and risks rebound ketoacidosis.

wrong_explanations.why: Bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidemia (pH <6.9) per consensus guidance; it is not indicated here and does not address the underlying insulin deficiency driving ketogenesis.

Decreasing insulin without adding dextrose risks under-treating ongoing ketogenesis; the correct pairing is dextrose supplementation, not dose reduction alone, while insulin delivery continues at an effective ketolytic rate.
Transition to subcutaneous insulin requires anion gap closure plus a 1-2 hour insulin overlap; switching now, with active ketoacidosis, risks rebound DKA from a gap in insulin coverage.
Stopping insulin entirely removes the agent suppressing lipolysis and ketogenesis; waiting 4 hours off insulin would allow ongoing acidosis and risk clinical deterioration.

question.difficulty_rationale: Requires recognizing that glucose improvement is a decoy — the true endpoint is anion gap closure — then applying the specific dextrose-plus-continued-insulin management rule rather than simply stopping or slowing insulin.
reasoning_steps: Recognize that DKA resolution is defined by anion gap/ketoacidosis closure, not glucose normalization
Note that glucose (175) has improved to near-normal while anion gap (19), bicarbonate (14), and beta-hydroxybutyrate remain abnormal
Understand that stopping or reducing insulin now would halt suppression of lipolysis and ketogenesis, risking rebound DKA
Apply the guideline rule: once glucose approaches ~200 mg/dL, add dextrose to IV fluids and continue insulin until the gap closes
Exclude bicarbonate (reserved for severe acidemia) and subcutaneous transition (requires gap closure plus insulin overlap) as premature

talk.key_point: DKA resolution is defined by closure of the anion gap and normalization of bicarbonate, not by glucose level; once glucose approaches 200 mg/dL, add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue insulin until the gap closes.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Insulin Infusion Management and Resolution Criteria

board_pearls: Insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis faster relative to its glucose-lowering effect being outpaced by fluid/insulin-driven glucose clearance — so glucose normalizes before the anion gap closes.
Per the ADA/AACE Hyperglycemic Crises Consensus Statement (2009), DKA resolution requires glucose <200 mg/dL AND two of: bicarbonate ≥15 mEq/L, venous pH >7.3, anion gap ≤12 [1].
The key discriminator from simply stopping insulin: add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue (not discontinue) the insulin infusion to sustain ketone clearance while preventing hypoglycemia.

Transition to subcutaneous insulin should only occur after DKA resolution criteria are met, with a 1-2 hour overlap between subcutaneous dosing and infusion discontinuation to prevent a gap in insulin coverage.
Common trap: treating glucose as the sole marker of DKA resolution and stopping insulin prematurely, which risks rebound ketoacidosis from unopposed lipolysis.
teaching_points: DKA resolution criteria are biochemical (anion gap, bicarbonate, pH), not glucose-based.
Dextrose-containing fluids should be added once glucose approaches 200 mg/dL to allow continued insulin administration without hypoglycemia.
Insulin infusion should not be stopped until ketoacidosis has resolved; subcutaneous insulin is started with overlap only after resolution.
summary_points: In DKA, continue IV insulin (adding dextrose as glucose falls) until the anion gap closes rather than stopping insulin once glucose normalizes.

visual_memory_card.bottom_left: DKA resolves by gap closure, not glucose level
visual_memory_card.bottom_right: Stopping insulin at normal glucose risks rebound DKA

gemini_errors: Board pearl states 'Insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis faster relative to its glucose-lowering effect...' — this is garbled and reverses the physiology described in its own explanation; the teaching point is that glucose falls before ketoacidosis clears.

Claims the 2009 ADA/AACE hyperglycemic crises consensus statement was 'reaffirmed in ADA Standards of Care 2025'; the 2009 statement has been superseded by the 2024 ADA/EASD Consensus Report on Hyperglycemic Crises, which is what the 2025 Standards reference — a citation-fidelity error.

Uses the outdated 2009 framework throughout (dextrose at ~200 mg/dL, bicarbonate only for pH <6.9, resolution requiring glucose <200 plus two of three) without acknowledging the 2024 update (dextrose at <250 mg/dL, target glucose 150–200, BHB-based resolution, bicarbonate consideration at pH <7.0).
Wrong-answer explanation for C ('decreasing insulin risks under-treating ongoing ketogenesis') contradicts the stem explanation, which endorses reducing to 0.02–0.05 U/kg/hr.
claude_errors: Resolution criteria are stated disjunctively ('anion gap ≤12, bicarbonate 15–18 or greater, pH >7.3, OR BHB <0.6 mmol/L'), implying any single criterion defines resolution; the 2024 ADA/EASD report requires BHB <0.6 mmol/L (or gap closure if ketones unavailable) TOGETHER WITH venous pH >7.3 or bicarbonate ≥15–18 mmol/L.
Teaching point states insulin should be held for K <3.3 mEq/L; this is the 2009 threshold — the 2024 ADA/EASD consensus cited as the primary source uses K <3.5 mEq/L.

Distractor C is framed as categorically wrong, but reducing the infusion to ~0.05 U/kg/h when dextrose is added is an accepted, guideline-sanctioned adjustment; the flaw in the option is omission of dextrose, not dose reduction per se (the explanation only partly makes this distinction).
judge.why: Both reach the same correct answer (add dextrose, continue insulin) and teach the core principle that DKA resolution is biochemical, not glycemic. A is anchored to the current 2024 ADA/EASD consensus with accurate thresholds (dextrose <250 mg/dL, target glucose 150–200, BHB monitoring preferred, resolution parameters), includes a computable anion gap and richer high-yield extensions (euglycemic DKA, potassium rules, subcutaneous overlap), and its citations plausibly support each claim. B relies on the superseded 2009 statement and inaccurately asserts it was reaffirmed in the 2025 Standards, contains a physiologically garbled pearl that contradicts its own explanation, and has an internal inconsistency between the explanation (reduce to 0.02–0.05 U/kg/hr) and distractor C. A wins on guideline currency, citation honesty, and teaching depth.

talk.title: Iron Deficiency Anemia
talk.subtitle: Iron homeostasis, hepcidin biology, and a mechanism-driven approach to workup and repletion
guideline_sources: ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Iron Deficiency Anemia (2020)
AABB Restrictive Transfusion Threshold (2023)
